bio.en: Jason Shah is a product leader whom Lenny worked with at Airbnb and who later led product in Web3; he shares deep, tactical advice on leadership, hiring, pushing back on your CEO, and advancing your career.
bio.zh: Jason Shah 是一位产品负责人，Lenny 曾在 Airbnb 与他共事，他后来也在 Web3 领域领导产品；他分享了关于领导力、招聘、如何对 CEO 说“不”、以及职业晋升的深入而具体的建议。

summary.en: Jason reframes 'pushback' as a negative word that puts you in a mindset of disagreeing, and instead advocates shifting direction or helping the business succeed when you disagree. He shares what it's like to be a PM in Web3 through crypto winter, how to lead a team through ups and downs while keeping morale and focus, and a wealth of advice on leadership, hiring, pushing back, working backwards, and career advancement. The episode is full of 'juicy' practical wisdom for product leaders at any stage.
summary.zh: Jason 把“pushback（顶撞/反对）”重新定义为一个负面词汇，会让人陷入“必须不同意”的心态，他主张在意见相左时改为“调整方向”或“帮助业务成功”。他分享了在加密寒冬中做 Web3 PM 是怎样的体验、如何在起伏中领导团队并保持士气与专注，以及大量关于领导力、招聘、向上管理、逆向工作与职业晋升的建议。这期节目充满对各阶段产品领导者都实用的“干货”。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Pushback is, I couldn't imagine a word more viscerally that makes you feel like you're sort of physically going against what somebody else wants, and it gears people into a mindset of then, well, how should I push back. It starts from a place of I need to disagree, I need to say no. It's a very negative mindset, purely based on the word that has come to label a behavior that alternatively could be about how do I shift the direction on something, or how do I help the business actually succeed when I disagree with somebody about something, and that's a very different mindset. And so, the two things that I've seen be most successful would be, I think number one is actually understanding what a goal is or what somebody's kind of issue is with something, and then actually aligning those things in some way.
turns.zh: 所谓"反抗"（pushback），我简直无法想象还有比这更直观的词汇，能让你真切感受到自己在身体上反抗他人意愿。它会让人们陷入一种思维模式——好吧，那我该如何反击呢？这种心态源自于"我必须反对"、"我必须说不"的负面情绪。这种心态完全基于这个词汇所标注的行为本质，而这种行为本质本可以被解读为：我该如何改变事物的方向？又或者当我与他人意见不合时，如何助力业务成功？这才是截然不同的思维模式。因此，我见过最成功的两种方法，一是真正理解目标或他人存在的核心问题，二是以某种方式将这些问题统一起来。

I was lucky to work with Jason while I was at Airbnb, and when I started working on this podcast, I knew that I wanted to have Jason on. He was actually my very first guest on this podcast when I was pre-recording some episodes, but as you'll hear in our chat, we decided to take another crack at it for reasons you'll soon understand.

We also get into a ton of killer advice on leadership, hiring, pushing back on your CEO, working backwards, career advancement, and a lot more juicy stuff. Jason is a gem and I am really excited to share this episode with you. With that, I bring you Jason Shah.

turns.zh: 约翰，跟我们讲讲 Amplitude 的幕后故事吧。大多数人提到 Amplitude 时，想到的都是产品分析，但如今你们正涉足实验领域，甚至刚刚推出了 CDP（客户数据平台）。背后的考量是什么？

turns.zh: 是的。Amplitude 始终以客户需求为导向。我们刚刚推出了入门模板，还为初创公司设立了优秀奖学金项目。当下正是推动增长的黄金时期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely agree. Thanks for joining us, John, and head to amplitude.com to get started. Jason, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。感谢约翰做客播客。访问 amplitude.com 即可立即上手。杰森，欢迎加入我们。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Thanks so much, Lenny. Really excited to chat with you today.
turns.zh: 非常感谢，莱尼。今天很高兴能与你交流。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something listeners don't know that we know is that we actually recorded an episode between you and I back in April. It was actually my very first episode that I ever did for this podcast, and it was before I launched. It was kind of like a pre-launch launch episode, and interestingly enough, by the time the podcast launched and it was going to go out, well, let me also add that we chatted mostly about Web3, forgot that detail. So, most of our chat was about Web3 in the state of Web3 and PMing in Web3, and by the time the podcast's supposed to come out, Web3, things have changed in the world of Web3, and so, it kind of felt a little stale and out of touch, and so, we decided let's do it again. And so, how do you feel about that?
turns.zh: 听众可能不知道的是，我们在四月份就录制过你我之间的对话。那是我的首期播客，也是推出前最后的预热特辑。有趣的是，当节目正式上线时，我们主要聊了 Web3，但当时 Web3 领域已风云变幻。所以那期内容显得有些过时且脱节，于是我们决定重新录制。你怎么看？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I appreciate that, Lenny. I'm honored that you would have me back. I'm going to count it as the personal record of two times on Lenny's Podcast, even if the world only knows it as one.
turns.zh: 很感激，莱尼。很荣幸能再次做客。算是我在 Lenny 播客上的两次亮相吧，即便外界只知道有一次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Good one. Okay, first ever guest and first two-time return guest. Amazing. Okay. To set a little context for folks on your background, your career, could you just give us a 60-second overview of your background and your career and how you got to what you're doing today?
turns.zh: 哇。不错。好的，首位嘉宾，也是首位两次回归的嘉宾。太棒了。接下来为大家简单介绍下你的背景和职业生涯，你是如何走到今天这一步的？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Yeah, for sure. Thanks again for having me, Lenny. So, my career has all been about solving important problems in a unique way. I think the latter part is the youngest child in me who has to be special and do things different than other people, and the former is about making sure that my time is spent well since we're all limited there. So, I actually got started in a sense in tech when I was 15. I started my first company, much like a lot of teenagers, it was around test prep and getting people ready for college, and it was my first exposure to using technology at scale to help people, and I just found it addictive ever since.
turns.zh: 是的，当然。再次感谢你邀请我，莱尼。说到我的职业生涯，一直致力于以独特方式解决重要问题。我觉得后者源于我作为老幺的性格——总想与众不同，用不同于他人的方法做事。而前者则关乎如何高效利用有限的时间。事实上，我15岁就开始涉足科技领域了。当时我创办了自己的第一家公司，和许多青少年一样，做的是考试备考辅导业务，帮助人们为上大学做准备。这是我首次大规模运用科技帮助他人的经历，从那以后我就深深着迷于此。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: And so, I ran that company for seven years through school, was lucky to do a small acquisition to a partner of ours that we had worked with throughout, and then I would just hooked, and I moved to San Francisco without a job. I was really arrogant. I said, "I'll never work for anybody else," and then lo and behold, Yammer comes along, I'm super excited about it, I had been working on a product actually in the same space. And so, that was actually my first formal product management role, and I stayed at Yammer, I stayed through the Microsoft acquisition back in 2012. Low and behold, I was at the world's largest productivity company at Microsoft, and most people there in my opinion were wildly unproductive and I wasn't shipping a lot. I got the itch again, so started another company called do.com and ran that for about four years, and then eventually, we found a better fit with Amazon. They were growing their AWS offering, SAS products. So, we partnered with them to kind of do a small acqui-hire and help build the team out and the product there for a little over a year.
turns.zh: 后来，我在求学期间继续经营这家公司。幸运的是，我们成功将公司出售给一位合作伙伴。之后我满怀激情地搬到了旧金山，尽管当时没有工作机会，却仍信誓旦旦地说：“我绝不会为别人打工。”结果Yammer找上了我，我对这个平台的热情简直爆棚，因为我之前就曾开发过类似产品。这实际上是我第一份正式的产品管理工作，直到2012年微软收购Yammer后，我才加入微软。说实话，当时微软是全球最大的生产力公司，但在我看来，大多数员工效率低下，我自己的项目进展也很缓慢。于是我再次萌生创业冲动，创办了do.com，运营了约四年。后来，我们与亚马逊达成了合作，帮助他们构建AWS和SAS产品。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: And then again, to be honest, I got bored and excited about what Airbnb was doing and the mission around belonging. That's why I was lucky to meet you and so many other really wonderful product leaders and just human beings in general at their core, and then to keep things brief for now, I got to work on a lot of really exciting products and businesses there, but eventually got the itch for Web3 after being a kind of observer from afar, investor, and I wanted to be a builder in Web3 specifically, and to me, it's a new vision of a better version of the internet. I'm really excited about that. So, I've been with Alchemy which is a blockchain infrastructure company for the last year, and really excited about all the opportunities. I've gotten to work on products that have been part of most people's everyday lives, and I'm hopeful that we'll get to do that with Web3 and Alchemy as well.
turns.zh: 再后来，说实话，我对Airbnb的使命和归属感理念深感兴趣。这让我有幸结识了你和许多优秀的产品领袖，以及许多真诚善良的人。目前先简单说一下，我在那里参与了许多令人兴奋的产品和业务开发，但最终被Web3技术吸引，尽管此前我只是作为旁观者和投资者关注着这一领域。我特别想亲身参与Web3的建设，对我而言，这是一个重构更美好互联网的新愿景。我对此充满期待。过去一年，我在区块链基础设施公司Alchemy工作，非常期待未来的机遇。我们的产品已融入大多数人的日常生活，我相信Web3和Alchemy也能带来同样的改变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I just realized as you're chatting there, do.com, I'm pretty sure I used that back in the day. I think I just realized that.
turns.zh: 太棒了。你说do.com，我突然意识到自己以前用过这个产品。我现在才想起来。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I hope so. That would be a new, I'll add that to my second podcast achievement is if I got Lenny to use a product that I worked on, especially a startup.
turns.zh: 希望如此吧。如果能让莱尼用上我参与开发的产品，特别是创业项目，那将是我的第二个播客成就了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Cool. Okay, so we're going to go a little bit backwards through your career and start with Web3. We're not going to spend most of the time on Web3, but just thought it'd be good to chat about some of these things, partly because you guest authored the sixth most popular post, online newsletter of all time, currently at number six, and it was about how to be a PM in Web3. Basically it's called The Product Manager's Guide to Web3. And so, a few questions there I wanted to touch on. One is just like, how would you describe the current state of Web3? We're recording this at the end of July, and so, we'll see when this comes out. But I'm just curious from someone working within it, kind of going through the boom and the busts, not the bust, the winter that we're kind of in a little bit right now. Yeah, how do you feel about it right now?
turns.zh: 哇。太酷了。好的，接下来我们要回顾一下你的职业生涯，从Web3说起。我们不会把大部分时间花在Web3上，但觉得还是有必要聊聊这个话题，部分原因是你的客座文章《Web3产品经理指南》在网络新闻通讯中排名第六，目前仍位列前六。这篇文章探讨了如何在Web3中担任产品经理。接下来，我想提几个问题：首先，你如何看待Web3目前的状态？我们在7月底录制这期节目，等节目播出后再看实际效果如何。但作为深耕其中的从业者，你如何看待Web3在经历繁荣与低谷后的现状？特别是我们当前所处的冬季阶段。嗯，你现在对它有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Yeah, for sure. So, as much as I'm a techno optimist, I'm also realist, and with that being said, I genuinely believe Web3 is in the strongest position that it's ever been in. I think it's important to remember that the term Web3 has barely existed in kind of popular lexicon for barely a year. We've definitely had crypto for more than a decade now as technology, arguably as a financial instrument of some sort, but specifically the number of companies that I'm seeing be formed, the number of products that are starting to actually achieve some form of early product market fit, some products that are starting to scale. There's definitely been obviously a huge drop in price. There's definitely been some huge scandals in terms of financial mismanagement and the contagion from that.
turns.zh: 嗯，肯定的。虽然我是个技术乐观主义者，但我也是个现实主义者。说真的，我认为Web3目前处在有史以来最强势的阶段。要知道，“Web3”这个术语在大众语境中流行还不到一年。诚然，加密货币作为技术存在已有十多年了，甚至可以说它是某种金融工具。但就我观察到的公司数量、产品开始实现早期产品市场适配的数量，以及部分产品开始规模化的情况而言，Web3确实正迎来重要机遇。当然，价格暴跌不可否认，金融管理不善引发的丑闻也带来了负面影响。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: But I think it's been my experience that a lot of new technologies don't move up in a straight line, and Web3 is especially challenging here because so many things have been financialized from the outset, whereas generally speaking, you'll see startups or new technologies mature over many years, whether it's the internet itself, artificial intelligence, QR codes, all sorts of things that kind of have gone through different periods of adoption, and so, I think we're seeing things kind of record Ethereum transactions happening, new Layer 2 technologies launching all the time that are going to help scale Layer 1 Blockchains, Solana has announced its phone that's going to be the first sort of Web3 native phone out there. So, there's so many new exciting product developments and users entering the space that as much as prices have come down, I'm really optimistic about the state of Web3.
turns.zh: 但根据我的经验，新技术的发展并非一帆风顺。Web3尤其具有挑战性，因为从一开始就有很多东西被金融化了。相比之下，初创公司或新技术通常需要多年发展才能成熟——无论是互联网本身、人工智能、二维码等技术，都经历了不同的采用阶段。所以，我认为我们正见证以太坊交易量创纪录，新二层技术不断推出，帮助一层区块链扩容，Solana宣布推出首款原生Web3手机。尽管价格下跌，但我对Web3的现状仍持乐观态度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think about a little bit is going through this shift in excitement about Web3 as a PM within a company working in this space, I imagine it tests some of the core skills of a PM, like keeping people focused, prioritizing effectively, keeping morale up. If people are getting like, "Oh man, all my cryptos going down," I'm curious how you've been able to leverage those skills and what you've learned going through this experience, keeping people focused, morale up, prioritizing effectively, those sorts of things.
turns.zh: 作为在该领域工作的产品经理，我想谈谈对Web3兴奋度的转变。这对PM的核心技能提出了考验，比如保持团队专注、有效分配优先级、维系士气。比如当人们说“天哪，我的加密货币都暴跌了”时，我很好奇你如何运用这些技能，以及从这段经历中学到了什么——如何保持专注、提振士气、有效分配优先级等等。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great question. It's really important, right, because we've seen in this space that there are these cycles, and I think that morale and ability to keep building are the determinants of long-term success, and if everybody kind of takes the ball and goes home, that uncertain future won't necessarily materialize. So, in my opinion, I think that the only way to maintain moral is to make progress. I think that no speech, no sort of extrinsic motivators like we're going to give everybody some free crypto to keep motivated about it or something like that really works. I think people get really excited when they see progress.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实是个很棒的问题。这真的很重要，对吧？因为我们在这个领域看到过周期性波动，我认为士气和持续建设的能力是长期成功的决定性因素。如果每个人都选择放弃，未来的不确定性就不会必然实现。所以，在我看来，保持士气的唯一方法就是取得进展。我认为任何演讲、任何外在激励措施——比如给每个人发些免费加密货币来保持积极性之类的——都行不通。当人们看到进展时，他们才会真正兴奋起来。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, for example, at Alchemy, we see more developers than we've ever had on the platform today, and then we're shipping, we just launched Solana support and people are like, "This is real." We're actually doing things, building things. We just had our team out at EthCC which is a big conference in Paris for the Ethereum community, and it was wild the number of people that were there, products being built. Pretty much every crypto conference has a hackathon, and so, it keeps the spirit of building so alive.
turns.zh: 举个例子，在Alchemy，我们今天看到平台上的开发者比以往任何时候都多，而且我们正在上线产品，比如刚刚推出的Solana支持功能，人们都感叹“这才是真材实料”。我们确实在做实事，在搭建产品。我们刚派团队参加了在巴黎举行的以太坊社区大会EthCC，那里人山人海，众多产品正在开发中。几乎每场加密货币大会都有黑客马拉松，这让建设的热情始终高涨。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: And so, I think it at Alchemy and just in other situations that I've been in as a leader over time, I think it's all about a focus on progress and moving forward. We saw this at Airbnb when the business had a draw down in revenue, and I know you'd covered this with Sanchan recently, right? It was 85, 90% revenue and you didn't know when it was going to turn around, right? It's not just like, "Oh yeah, this will come back in six months and we can just keep plowing forward." But I think what worked was making progress and actually focusing on product and your customers, and ultimately if you hire the right people who are motivated for the right reasons, I think that recipe keeps people highly motivated and highly effective at building for when things do eventually turn around.
turns.zh: 所以，无论是在Alchemy，还是我作为领导者长期参与的其他项目中，我认为关键在于专注于进展和向前推进。我们在Airbnb看到过，当业务收入下滑时（我知道你最近和Sanchan聊过这个，对吧？收入曾降至85%、90%，而且不知道何时能回升），并不是说只要等着“六个月后就会回升，然后我们就能继续前进”。但我认为有效的方法是取得进展，真正专注于产品和客户，最终如果招到因正确理由而积极主动的人才，士气和效率就能得到极大提升，等待形势好转时就能顺势而为。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of the most interesting and maybe surprising points you made in the post that you wrote about being a PM in Web3 is that there's much less need for a PM, especially early stage Web3, and it feels like, the stuff you're talking about feels like a PM's really helpful along these lines. So, I'm curious, are things changing at all there? Have you changed your perspective on PMs and Web3, and then I don't know, where do you see the evolution of product management and Web3?
turns.zh: 你在《Web3中的产品经理》一文中提到，Web3早期阶段对产品经理的需求较低，这或许令人惊讶。但你现在在产品管理和Web3领域的观点是否有所变化？你对Web3中的产品管理和PM角色的演变有何看法？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I actually am seeing things change a lot, and one thing in Web3, if one learns nothing is the ability to admit when they're wrong or when things change. And so, I think that that's exactly what I'm seeing. So, basically, I'm specifically noticing a lot of teams hiring product leaders, more product managers. Those product managers are actually now working kind of increasingly in sort of more traditional product management fashion, in addition to some of the differences that we discussed in the post around the community management and role in marketing and things like this, but specifically, Uniswap just made a big hire out of Meta. I saw that Gemini also did the same. We're seeing OpenSea hire a lot of talent along these lines too, even through the ups and downs that their business has seen, and at all levels. Whether it's kind of product manager, senior product manager, director, VP or CPO, you're seeing it across the board.
turns.zh: 我确实看到很多变化。Web3的一个关键点在于，学会在错误或环境变化时承认失败。这正是我所观察到的。具体来说，越来越多的团队在招聘产品负责人，尤其是初创阶段的Web3公司。这些产品经理现在不仅在产品管理的传统领域工作，还在社区管理、市场营销等领域发挥作用。但最显著的是，Uniswap刚从Meta挖来高管，Gemini也做了同样的举动。OpenSea也在大规模招聘人才，尽管其业务经历了起起落落，且招聘范围涵盖各级职位——从产品经理、资深产品经理，到总监、VP和CPO等职位。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: And so, I think that's partially happening because you're seeing a maturation of products, right, and so, maybe you can start early with a few engineers, a community manager, get the ball rolling, but eventually the product is more mature, the complexity has grown, the role of the product manager is far more useful than they can differentiate. I also think the market is getting increasingly competitive. So, there's many NFT marketplaces. There's many Layer 1 and Layer 2 blockchains. As a result, I think product is always a competitive advantage, right? If it's working, it improves strategy, it improves execution, and improves team collaboration. And so, maybe that was less of a difference maker before where these teams didn't need that competitive advantage as much because maybe they launched a token and the token was mooning, and so a bunch of people were adopting the product, but that only lasts so long, and first principles still come come in to focus, whether it's one day or one month from now.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为这种情况的部分原因在于产品正在走向成熟，对吧？所以，也许你可以早期先招几位工程师和一位社区经理，推动项目启动，但最终产品会变得更加复杂，产品经理的角色比以往任何时候都更有价值，他们需要区分不同的优先级。我还认为市场竞争越来越激烈了。现在有很多NFT市场平台，还有很多第一层和第二层区块链项目。因此，产品始终是竞争优势，对吧？如果产品运行良好，它能优化战略、提升执行力，并促进团队协作。也许在过去，这不是那么关键，因为这些团队不需要那么多的竞争优势——比如他们推出一个代币，代币价格暴涨，然后一大批人就开始使用这个产品，但这种情况不会持续太久，最终还是要回归到第一性原理，无论是今天还是一个月后。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, I'm definitely seeing it shift. It's definitely making a huge, positive difference in the cases that I've observed, and my hunch is we're only going to continue to observe this because with more user adoption comes new challenges, and for all these players that are growing and getting some form of adoption, the product complexity is only going to grow, and having somebody to help lead teams, help prioritize between all the different products that they could build or strategies they could pursue is going to only increase in importance.
turns.zh: 所以，我确实看到这种转变。在我观察到的案例中，这确实带来了巨大的积极影响。我预感这种趋势还会持续下去，因为随着用户数量增加，新的挑战也会随之而来。对于所有正在发展并获得一定用户认可的项目来说，产品复杂度只会不断攀升，因此，帮助团队优先排序、在众多可开发的产品或可实施的战略中做出取舍的角色，将变得越发重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know we're like we're PM people talking about the value of PM, but something I find is that people that are kind of anti having a PM or don't see why they need a PM in my experience just haven't worked with a great product manager because my experience, you find a great PM, they just make everything better, and so, it's not surprising to hear what you're sharing which is people are kind of discovering that value of bringing on a product manager, even if it's mostly engineering work. And so, that's promising, and I wonder if that's just a natural evolution of a new space where people are like, "Eh, I don't need PMs in this one," and then like, "Oh, okay, well, I see. All these things aren't happening. We need someone to help. Who can do that for us? Maybe it's a PM."
turns.zh: 我知道我们是产品经理，谈论产品经理的价值，但我发现，那些反对引入产品经理或不明白其必要性的人，大多是因为他们没有遇到过优秀的产品经理。在我的经验中，优秀的产品经理能让一切更顺畅。因此，听到你分享的观点并不意外——人们逐渐意识到引入产品经理的价值，哪怕只是处理工程任务。这很令人欣慰，我好奇这是否是新领域的自然演进。最初人们会说“在这种情况下不需要产品经理”，然后又意识到“哦，原来需要啊。我们需要有人来帮忙。或许就是产品经理。”

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Yeah, that's a great observation. I think that combination of having a direct need for something that emerges as well as if somebody's had either a bad experience or not even had any experience with somebody who can play this role which is quite common in Web3, especially because a lot of folks are relatively early in their career, given the kind of accessibility of the space, and I think frankly the more adept understanding of the space naturally that a lot of people have when they're early in their career and less set in their ways. And so, that's a great point, and as a result, the better PMs we see in Web3, hopefully the value will prove itself out over time.
turns.zh: 是的，这是一个很棒的观察。我认为既有对新兴需求的直接满足，也有人们对产品经理角色的体验不足——这在Web3领域很常见，尤其是因为许多人职业生涯较早，又因为该领域的开放性，他们往往对技术栈有更深的理解，但也更容易被既有思维框架束缚。这是个很好的观察结果，希望Web3领域的优秀产品经理能随着时间证明自己的价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And hopefully they do well so people don't keep getting burned out by bad PMs.
turns.zh: 希望他们能做得出色，这样人们就不会再被糟糕的产品经理拖累了。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: We're rooting for all PMs, but definitely Web3 PMs too.
turns.zh: 我们为所有产品经理加油，但尤其为Web3的产品经理加油。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. What's surprised you most about working in Web3 as a PM?
turns.zh: 是的。在Web3担任产品经理，最让你惊讶的是什么？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I mean, I think that the biggest surprise to me, despite what we were just talking about, was how big some products have gotten without kind of the traditional either product manager role or without the playbooks that we're so used to from the last 20 years of the internet. And so, for example, Uniswap has done more daily volume on certain days than Coinbase, and Uniswap is about a hundred people versus 5,000-plus at Coinbase, right? So, that's astounding to me.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，尽管我们刚刚讨论了这些问题，但最让我惊讶的是，许多产品在没有传统产品经理角色、也没有我们过去20年在互联网领域习惯的流程手册的情况下，就做得如此之大。举个例子，Uniswap某些日子的交易量比Coinbase还要高，而Uniswap只有大约100名员工，而Coinbase则有5000多名员工，对吧？这让我感到震惊。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I think a lot of these NFT collections and communities that have grown. I met with a lot of these at NFT.NYC recently, and a lot of them, aside from the price speculation and things like this, have actually built, the Bored Ape Yacht Club is actually building a metaverse project that does look better than some of the digital games that I've used in the past of Second Life and things like this. Obviously, a lot of time has passed and so there's a greater foundation of technology to build off of and they're working with a partner on that product as well, but there's a ton of progress being made without some of the traditional product structure or individuals. And so, again, I think PMs play a really strong role, but it's been incredibly surprising to see how far products can get without the product playbooks and resources that somebody who's worked in the internet space from the last 10 or 20 years is so used to.
turns.zh: 我认为许多NFT系列和社区的成长令人惊叹。我最近在NFT.NYC上与许多这些社区进行了交流。除了价格投机等因素外，其中许多社区实际上已经建立了自己的基础设施。比如，Bored Ape Yacht Club正在开发的元宇宙项目，看起来比我过去使用过的Second Life等数字游戏要先进得多。显然，时间已经过去了很久，现在有更坚实的技术基础可供借鉴，他们还在与合作伙伴共同开发这个项目，但即使没有传统的产品结构或专业人员，项目也能取得巨大进展。所以，我认为产品经理确实发挥着重要作用，但看到产品在没有产品手册和资源的情况下也能取得如此大的成就，这实在令人惊讶，尤其是对于在过去10到20年里一直从事互联网行业的人来说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. We're going to move on from Web3 and chat a bit about some of your other career accomplishments and companies you've worked at. So, you worked at, you mentioned Yammer, Microsoft, Amazon, Airbnb. I'm curious which of those companies has most informed the way you approach product and build product and run teams because they're all so different in how they operate, and I'm always curious what company is the formative experience for you that's like, "Here's how I like to build product most." I know it's always a combination, but how do you think about that?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，接下来我们要从Web3转向聊聊你其他的职业成就和曾就职的公司。比如，你提到过Yammer、微软、亚马逊、Airbnb。我很好奇这些公司中哪一家最能影响你对待产品、构建产品和管理团队的方式，因为它们的运营方式截然不同，我一直很好奇哪家公司对你的影响最大，能让你说“这就是我最喜欢的产品构建方式”。我知道这通常是多方面因素的综合，但你怎么看呢？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Yeah, it's definitely a combination, but I would say if I had to pick, Amazon, even though I was only there for about a year after the acquisition. I say that because of this blend between product and business thinking that is especially present there. And so, people say Google is an engineering culture. People said Facebook is a product culture, Airbnb or Pinterest, sometimes a design culture or things like this, and I think that Amazon was a place where you couldn't divorce business and product. You couldn't be a product manager without thinking about revenue growth, without thinking about go to market, and I really like that because as a startup founder doing product in a bigger company, it gave me the chance to exercise a lot of those skills.
turns.zh: 是的，这确实是多方面因素的综合，但如果非要选一个的话，我会选亚马逊，尽管我在收购后只待了一年左右。我这么说是因为那里特别注重产品和商业思维的融合。人们说谷歌是工程师文化，Facebook是产品文化，Airbnb或Pinterest有时是设计文化等等，但我认为亚马逊是一个商业和产品不可分割的地方。如果你不考虑收入增长和市场推广，就不算产品经理。我真的很喜欢这种文化，因为作为在大公司做产品的初创企业创始人，这让我有机会锻炼这些技能。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: It's very similar actually to how I feel at Alchemy now where I remember my first month there I was like, people ask me how's it going, I'm like, "I feel like an athlete. I feel alive again." I can do M&A one day, I can be doing product another minute. I could be figuring out, oh, we need to hire our first lawyer to write onboarding plans for employees the next minute, and it wasn't as siloed as sometimes a product role can be. So, I think Amazon, I went there to learn and understand. That was my biggest goal was this is an incredible company that's gone into... The Whole Foods acquisition happened when I was there, and I was wondering how does the same company kind of within retail win with the AWS, go create studios, and I think the Amazon culture ultimately more than anything else around ownership, being vocally self-critical is right a lot as one of the leadership principles. All these things combined I think created a really unique culture.
turns.zh: 事实上，这和我在Alchemy的感受非常相似。我记得刚到那里的第一个月，我被问到进展如何，我回答：“我感觉自己像个运动员，又活力满满了。” 一天我可能在做并购项目，转头又投入产品开发。下一分钟我可能就在构思如何招聘首位律师来为新员工制定入职计划。这里不像有些产品岗位那样割裂。所以我认为亚马逊对我最大的影响，是让我去那里学习和理解。这家令人惊叹的公司在收购全食超市时我就身处其中，当时我就在思考同一家公司如何能在零售领域胜出，如何借助AWS开创工作室模式。我认为亚马逊的文化最核心的要素是赋予员工自主权，以及坦诚自我批评的领导力原则。所有这些因素共同造就了独特的文化。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, I would say Amazon's had the biggest impact on me, and there have been certain lessons that I've taken from, like you said, all these places, but Amazon was by far the place that I think left the biggest mark on my view on product and leadership.
turns.zh: 所以我会说亚马逊对我的影响最大。虽然我在其他地方也学到了一些东西，但亚马逊无疑是给我在产品和领导力观方面留下最深印象的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's quite amazing that you were there for a year and that's the one that's most informed and impacted you. Do you feel like people should try to go work at Amazon as a training ground as a PM? Is that something you encourage PM to try to do?
turns.zh: 你能在那里待一年，并且它对你影响最大，这真是令人惊叹。你觉得人们应该把亚马逊当作产品经理的培训基地吗？你是否鼓励产品经理尝试去亚马逊？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: In general, I certainly had a positive experience, but I think that as you know and as I'm sure you've advised countless people, it's so context dependent. Are you learning the zero to one? Are you learning the one to scale? What's your aspiration? Is somebody trying to start a company eventually, or are they trying to work the ranks of the product leadership trajectory? And so, I definitely enjoyed it a lot, and I think to your point, there's often a non-linear sort of correlation between factors that we traditionally think are linked, right? So, my time there was one of the shortest, but my learnings were some of the greatest because I was really intentional and maybe because of the sort of moment in time and what I wanted to get out of it.
turns.zh: 总的来说，我在那里的经历确实很积极，但正如你所知，也正如我相信你已经为无数人提供过建议的，这取决于具体背景。你是在学习从零到一的阶段吗？还是在学习从一到规模的阶段？你的抱负是什么？是有人想最终创办公司，还是想在产品领导力阶梯上逐步晋升？所以我确实非常享受那段经历，而且正如你所指出的，传统上认为相关联的因素之间往往存在非线性关联，对吧？所以我在那里的时间最短，但收获最多，因为我非常用心，也许还因为当时的时机和我的期望。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: The same way for what it's worth, while we're talking about this disconnect, when I went to Yammer, I also interviewed with kind of... This was the era of TaskRabbit. I talked to Square and I remember people always say, "Well, what stage do you want to join seed, Series A, Series B?" And the crazy thing is that Yammer was, it was already passed a hundred people, it grew to 500 by the time of the acquisition, and it felt almost like the culture was so tightknit, it felt like a seed stage company at some points, even though eventually it kind of felt like... Well, once it was acquired from Microsoft, we'll just say it didn't feel like a seed stage company anymore, but it felt smaller than a lot of the actual smaller companies than I was at. So, I think that's something I've noticed a lot is that a lot of the proxies don't necessarily match the internal realities in certain cases.
turns.zh: 同样值得一提的是，当我们谈论这种脱节时，当我去Yammer面试时，我也面试了其他公司。这是TaskRabbit时代。我和Square的人交谈，记得大家总是问：“你想加入种子轮、A轮还是B轮？”最疯狂的是，Yammer当时已经有100多人，被收购时增长到500人。感觉那里文化非常紧密，有时甚至像种子阶段的公司，尽管最终被微软收购后，那种感觉就不再像种子阶段公司了，但它比我待过的许多实际小公司还要小。所以我注意到很多表象并不一定与某些情况下的内部现实相符。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned you picked up a bunch of tactics and kind of lessons from some of these companies. What's one concrete process or tactic that you took it away from either Amazon or one of these other companies that stuck with you that you like to kind of share with folks?
turns.zh: 你提到从这些公司中学到了不少策略和经验教训。能否分享一个具体的流程或策略，无论是来自亚马逊还是其他公司，让你印象深刻且愿意与大家分享的？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Yeah, definitely. I mean, I think one that Amazon is well-known for is the working backwards process, and for those that don't know, the idea is try to define effectively an ideal end state which funnily enough is very similar to some of what we both experienced at Airbnb and took away, and usually the mechanism for doing this is what's called a PRFAQ, and that's a press release and frequently asked questions, and it forces a certain degree of clarity to have to actually write a press release about the product that you're going to eventually launch.
turns.zh: 当然可以。我觉得亚马逊闻名遐迩的一个策略是逆向设计流程。对于不了解的人来说，核心理念是先明确理想的终极状态，有趣的是，这与我们在Airbnb的经历颇为相似。通常实现这一目标的机制是PRFAQ，即新闻稿和常见问题解答。通过为即将推出的产品撰写新闻稿，迫使团队以极高的清晰度来定义产品愿景。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Every employee goes through actually like a business writing class after they start at Amazon. They give you a little card with five tips that you're supposed to keep on your desk about concision and specificity in the words you use. For example, you should never write the word great in an Amazon press release. You should write user friendly in X, Y, Z way and will save customers time 20 minutes each day through this. It's intended to be very concrete in a way that avoids some of the fluffiness that frankly... It's funny, when people try to move from slides to docs, they really just import the same mindsets that they use in slides, but just with more words now.
turns.zh: 在亚马逊入职后，每位员工都要参加商业写作课程。他们会发给员工一张卡片，上面有五条建议，要求放在办公桌上，提醒用词要简洁准确。例如，亚马逊的新闻稿绝不能用“很棒”这样的词汇，而应用“用户友好”这样的表述，并说明产品将如何为用户节省20分钟时间。这类指导旨在用具体数据避免空谈——说实话，当人们试图从幻灯片转向文档时，往往只是把幻灯片上的思维模式搬到文字里，但文字量反而更大了。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: And so, I think the working backwards process of establishing the long-term goal using a mechanism like a press release and the FAQs where every word matters, and even the FAQs, for what it's worth, there's a section for external FAQs that you would include for example as an appendix, but also internal FAQs that are meant to de-risk launch or raise the elephant in the room or dogs not barking as Amazon likes to call it often. So, that was a really helpful process that felt very true to me as a way I like to live my life as well, and then also very applicable.
turns.zh: 我认为逆向设计流程——通过新闻稿和FAQ等机制明确长期目标，字字珠玑。值得一提的是，FAQ还分为对外FAQ和对内FAQ。前者可作为附录，后者则用于规避产品发布风险、直击痛点（亚马逊常称为“把桌上的大象搬开”）。这个流程对我帮助极大，不仅与我的生活方式高度契合，也极具实用性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The tidbit about not using the word great is so interesting. Is there anything else there that you could share about just basically just like how to write effectively and communicate and launch. Is there any other tidbits along those lines?
turns.zh: 关于不使用“很棒”这个词的细节很有意思。还有其他关于有效沟通和产品发布的技巧吗？能否分享一些这方面的经验？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Yeah, that's a good question. In addition to not using the word great and words like it that are either subjective in what they mean or unclear in what they actually mean, definitely using numbers more than adjectives. Strict concision, I would go over these documents countless times, and there's a phrase, I can't remember, it's either Mark Twain or another famous writer who said kill your darlings, right? Cut, cut, cut, and just remove. And so, I think I found that really useful in emails I write or documents I write to this day is just going over, not because you're saving ink by cutting words, but because it forces clarity of thought. Fewer words means every word is 10 pounds in weight instead of one, and that means that the decisions you're making, the trade offs are far more intentional, and in the case of great, if you say something is great because we're going to deliver something in two hours versus Amazon's great because the selection is very wide, the implications on strategy are completely different. And so, that's one of the benefits of being very specific and very concrete in language.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实是个好问题。除了避免使用“很棒”之类的词汇——因为这些词要么带有主观色彩，要么意思模糊——之外，还有一点很重要，那就是要多用数字而非形容词。保持极度简洁，我会反复校对这些文件。有一句话我记不太清了，可能是马克·吐温或其他知名作家说的“杀死你的宠儿”吧？不断删减、删减、再删减。就我而言，至今在写邮件或文件时，我都会反复检查——倒不是为了节省墨水，而是为了确保思维清晰。用词越少，每个字就越有分量。这意味着你做出的决策、权衡利弊的过程都必须经过深思熟虑。比如，“很棒”这个词，如果你说“我们两小时内就能送货上门，所以很棒”，而亚马逊说“我们的产品种类非常丰富，所以很棒”，两者的战略含义完全不同。所以，在用词上做到具体、明确，这确实有很大好处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I didn't intend to go too deep into this topic, but no one's ever covered this working backwards process on this podcast, so it's kind of interesting to talk about it a little bit more maybe. How does that actually work? So, you sit there and you actually write out a press release that would go out when you launch this thing. Is there like a template used? Is there anything you could share for folks that want to try this out and/or point them to a resource that will help them down this road?
turns.zh: 我本不打算深入探讨这个话题，但这个播客上从未有人谈及这种逆向思考的过程，或许多聊几句还是挺有意思的。具体流程是怎样的呢？比如，你会坐下来，实际撰写一份产品发布时会发布的新闻稿。是否有模板可用？有没有可以分享给想尝试的人的资源，或者指引他们去哪里寻找相关资料？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Yeah, definitely. That's a great question. So, there definitely is a template, and so, it's a combination of an internal training where you have to write one of these documents. You review kind of good, bad, medium versions of this. It's generally used if there's let's say a proposal for a new product or even a proposal to buy a company. This helps really simulate what it's going to be like.
turns.zh: 当然，这确实是个好问题。确实有模板存在，通常这是一个内部培训环节，要求参与者撰写此类文件。参与者会评估不同版本的优劣。这种模板主要用于新产品提案或收购提案等场景，能有效模拟真实场景。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: With respect to a template, what I recall is it was often sort of an introduction where you get kind of right to the point. You say what you're announcing. Then usually you would describe the problem in one paragraph and in very clear language. Again, all of the writing is this way. Then the solution, you briefly describe the product. After that, there's always a customer quote, and this is an example of this customer obsession that Amazon is so famous for that many companies like to say or emulate, but I think it really kind of may not be true if you evaluate the mechanisms that they use, for example, product specs that either don't have customer data or don't have quotes from customers, things like this. And so, there's a customer quote, and you have to literally put yourself into the shoes of... Let's say you were launching Prime. Put yourself in the shoes of Lenny from San Francisco. What exactly is he going to say when he has access to this, and how's it different than his life today, and what are the words that he's going to use?
turns.zh: 关于模板，我记得通常结构是开篇直切主题，说明发布内容。接下来用一段简洁明了的语言描述问题，再以同样的风格描述解决方案。最后要引用客户评价，体现亚马逊以客户为中心的理念。许多公司都标榜这种理念，但仔细观察其产品规格或客户评价，就会发现其所谓的客户导向可能存在问题。比如，产品规格中可能没有客户数据或引用语句。所以，引用客户评价时，必须设身处地为用户着想。比如，如果你要推出Prime会员服务，就要设想旧金山的Lenny会如何评价这项服务，与他当下的生活相比有何不同，以及他会用哪些词汇来表达？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You can't use great.
turns.zh: 不能用“很棒”这样的词汇。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I mean, if great is one of your favorite words, maybe you could stretch it, but I think if you were in a room with your peers at Amazon, they might put some red pen through any greats that are used there. So, I found that really helpful, and it also helps force out of this box that product managers, product leaders tend to get into of thinking that they are always the customer and being a little sort of intellectually lazy, where I'm like, "Yeah, I would like Prime, so let me write the quote for what I would like," but maybe I'm only a small segment within our total customer addressable market.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，如果"伟大"是你的最爱词汇之一，或许你可以把它延伸一下，但我觉得如果你在亚马逊的同行面前说出这个词，他们可能会用红笔划掉所有用词夸张的地方。所以，我觉得这真的很有帮助。它还能促使产品经理和产品负责人跳出思维定式，摆脱那种自以为永远代表用户、有些思维懒惰的观念。比如，我会想"我喜欢Prime会员服务，所以就按我的需求写需求文档"，但也许我只是整个潜在客户群中的一小部分。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, anyhow, there's a customer quote, then there's one leadership quote similarly that this achieves a complimentary goal, like how does this fit into our strategy in a way that you would express to the public but is still true to what the internal sensitivities and mechanisms would be. And then a call to action towards the end, and not just download here, but this will be available to customers next month. They can go access these portals within these Whole Food stores at this state. It again forces clarity of thought with respect to not only the rollout plan, but taking a step back. When you read it, do you feel like you would actually want this product? Would you use it? So, I found that really helpful as a structure.
turns.zh: 总之，先是客户的需求陈述，接着是领导层的表态，两者相辅相成。比如，这如何与我们的战略相契合？你如何向公众阐述，同时又忠实于内部的敏感性和机制？最后是行动号召——不是现在下载，而是下个月客户就能在全食超市的门店使用。这种结构不仅能理清发布计划的思路，还能退后一步审视全局。当你阅读这些内容时，是否会觉得自己真的会想要这个产品？会使用它吗？所以，我觉得这种结构非常有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you just summarize those again real quick?
turns.zh: 能不能快速再总结一下要点？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: For sure. So the structure of the PRFAQ docs was generally an introduction where you're announced the product, problem, solution, customer quote, leadership quote, and a call to action.
turns.zh: 当然可以。PRFAQ文档的结构通常是先介绍产品、问题、解决方案，再给出客户引述、领导层引述，最后是行动号召。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, interesting how similar that is to a one pager potentially. The other thought I had while you're chatting, so the Airbnb approach is work back from the ideal, Brian talks about it, the 11-star experience versus the Amazon approach which it doesn't need to be the ideal, it just needs to be an awesome launch. So, that's an interesting difference, both effective in different ways.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，这和单页文档的结构很相似。我在听你讲的时候还想到了Airbnb的做法——从理想状态出发。布莱恩提到过"11星级体验"与亚马逊的做法不同。亚马逊不需要追求完美，只需要确保成功发布。所以，这是两种有效的不同策略，各自有其优势。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I think people tend to, when they see that both companies have some sort of working backwards process of thought, I would say working backwards on one hand and then 11-star experience on the other. Listening to how you describe it, I want to almost frame it as working backwards from sort of a moment in time or a launch like you said with Amazon versus working backwards from a quality standard in some sense of an 11-star experience.
turns.zh: 我觉得人们往往会把两家公司的方法归为两类：一方面是倒推式思维，另一方面是11星级体验。听你描述后，我想把这两者框架化：一方面是从亚马逊的某个发布时刻倒推，另一方面是从11星级体验的质量标准倒推。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Going in a slightly different direction, one of the things I wanted to chat about is you worked at all these different companies and they have different types of leadership and different approaches to leadership. And so, I'm curious, what have you learned about effective leadership watching all these awesome operators work, and what kind of separates them in your experience from folks that maybe aren't as effective?
turns.zh: 再聊点不同的话题。你在这么多不同公司工作过，他们的领导力风格和方法各不相同。我很好奇，在观察这些优秀的管理者时，你学到了哪些高效领导的秘诀？在你看来，他们与那些不太高效的人有何不同？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great question, and to briefly recap, right, I've gotten to see somebody like David Sachs who've been the CEO of PayPal and then the founder of Yammer and gone to do many more things since then. I've gotten to see sort of Jeff Bezos at a distance. I was never that close to him obviously and never got to work with him, but got to observe his impact on the organization. Obviously, I've gotten to witness Brian Chesky and his leadership in sort of the pre-IPO days as well as through the ups and downs of COVID, and then also now at Alchemy, our co-founders, Joe and Nikil are leaders that have really had an impact on me as well, and I would count myself, but I've also see myself as a bad leader in the start of [inaudible 00:29:56] and learn from that.
turns.zh: 是的，这确实是个很棒的问题。简单回顾一下，我曾有机会见到像大卫·萨克斯这样的人——他曾担任PayPal的CEO，后来创立了Yammer，此后又投身于更多事业。我还远远地见过杰夫·贝索斯。虽然我显然从未与他密切合作过，但却目睹了他对组织的影响力。显然，我见证了布莱恩·切斯基在IPO前夕的领导力，以及他在新冠疫情期间的起起落落。如今在Alchemy，我们的联合创始人乔和尼基尔也是对我影响深远的领导者。我也认为自己曾是个糟糕的领导者——至少在[00:29:56缺失]初期是这样，并从中吸取了教训。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I think it's a really important thing to reflect on, and I think for me there are three things that have stood out the most. I think number one, nothing is above them. I've seen whether it's Brian caring about the full bleed image on the homepage, whether it's Jeff Bezos who famously would receive customer emails, read many of them, forward them, and he's famous for question mark emails where for his time's sake he would just forward an email to a leader with a question mark and you would just have to figure it out and then report back in 24 hours with the resolution thereof. But nothing's above them, and a lot of founders or a lot of CEOs or even CPOs and leaders think you get to a certain point and then I'm above a product spec, I'm above looking at the data running a sequel query, and I think that that is a mistake in a lot of ways, especially from a standpoint of who people come to respect as well as efficacy at one's job.
turns.zh: 我认为反思这一点非常重要，对我来说，最突出的有三点：首先，没有什么是高高在上的。无论是布莱恩关注主页上的满版图片，还是杰夫·贝索斯亲自阅读客户邮件、转发邮件并以问号邮件回复的做法——他会把邮件转发给高管，附上问号，让对方在24小时内给出解决方案。但没有什么是高高在上的，许多创始人、CEO、甚至首席产品官和领导者都认为，自己到了某个阶段就凌驾于产品规格之上，凌驾于查看数据、运行续集查询之上。我认为这种想法在很多方面都是错误的，尤其是在人们对领导者的尊重度以及工作效率方面。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: And then the other two things would be, I think they're in the details. So, it's less about being above something, but this is kind of Amazon's famous for auditing the details for example, and leaders are... For example, when we were going to launch Prime, order a bunch of Prime things and see what happens and really test things out, and write up a long feedback email on Saturday or something like that, and make sure that things are moving forward.
turns.zh: 另外两点则体现在细节上。与其说高高在上，不如说亚马逊以审计细节闻名。例如，当我们准备推出Prime会员服务时，会订购一堆Prime商品，观察效果，并在周六写一封长长的反馈邮件，确保一切进展顺利。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, I think in my opinion, some of the best leaders, David Sachs would do this too. He actually ran the product reviews. It was the CEO of the company doing product reviews, not some kind of middle tier of a director of product who was just running them. They were force involved and there were things to delegate and activate around, but Sachs was in all of those details and ran those product reviews himself and would talk to the product managers directly, and I think that was really impactful, and it also, I think from an accountability and culture perspective, when you're PM and you talk to the CEO and you feel like you're presenting something at product review, it's totally different, and it creates a certain amount of responsibility and quality, frankly, that I think is really important, and it's a way to coach obviously as well for those leaders to really make a mark on the organization.
turns.zh: 在我看来，像大卫·萨克斯这样的优秀领导者也会这样做。他实际上亲自负责产品评审。作为公司的CEO亲自参与产品评审，而不是让某个中层产品总监来负责。他们会亲自参与其中，有许多事情需要分配和推动，但萨克斯会深入到所有细节中，亲自主持产品评审，并直接与产品经理沟通。我认为这非常有影响力，从问责和文化的角度来看，当你作为产品经理与CEO交谈，感觉自己是在产品评审中展示成果时，效果截然不同。这会产生一定的责任感和质量意识，我认为这非常重要，同时也是对这些领导者进行指导的一种方式，让他们真正在组织中留下深刻印记。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: And then lastly, I think they adapt, right? I think that are a lot of leaders who are like, "I've worked 20 years to become a leader in this way and I have a playbook," either based on past experience or based on some sort of philosophy that they've developed over time that they feel committed to in some way, and I think coming back to some of these examples of watching Brian lead through COVID or watching Joe and Nikil now through this particular crypto winter shift gears and figure out exactly like we're still building the core business, but how else can we lean into this and adapt to the unique opportunities that are in front of us. I think that's really powerful. So, what I've seen is nothing is above them, they're in the details, and they adapt to new information and new situations. That's what I've seen the most that I've appreciated in the best leaders that I've gotten to either observe or work closely with.
turns.zh: 最后，我认为他们会适应变化，对吧？我觉得有很多领导者会说：“我花了20年才成为这样的领导者，我有一套固定的策略”，无论是基于过去的经验，还是基于他们多年来形成并深信不疑的某种理念。我认为回顾布莱恩在新冠疫情期间的领导表现，或者乔和尼基尔在当前加密货币寒冬中的应对策略，都很能说明问题——他们始终坚持核心业务发展，同时灵活把握机遇。我认为这才是真正的领导力。就我观察到的最优秀的领导者而言，他们无所不能，注重细节，能够灵活应对新信息和新情况。这才是我最欣赏他们的地方，无论是作为观察者还是合作伙伴，我都深有体会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That's super interesting. The first two are kind of connected which is really interesting, and it just reminds me of Brian and how detail-oriented he was about everything. He used to review every product launch and every screen of every new product. We had to show him here's what we're launching this week, and he just kind of went through and either blew it up or let it pass. And then I just remember the founders, when they were designing the office space, just looking at pictures of listings they wanted to... Because Airbnb, the office conference rooms were modeled after Airbnb listings, and Jim just looking through hundreds of listings that the team brought him and he'd just picked the ones that he wanted to turn into conference rooms. Also, obviously Steve Jobs. This is a really interesting through line of great leaders is just this huge attention to detail, and there's probably something about once they let go that thing start to kind of diminish. Is that what you find?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这真的很有趣。前两个例子之间有某种关联，非常有意思，这让我想起了布莱恩，他对所有事情都要求极其细致。他过去会审查每一次产品发布，每个新产品的每个界面。我们得向他展示本周要上线的产品，他会逐一审视，要么大加赞赏，要么直接否决。我还记得创始人们在设计办公室空间时，会翻看Airbnb房源的图片，因为Airbnb的办公室会议室是仿照Airbnb房源设计的，吉姆会翻看团队收集的数百个房源图片，从中挑选出他想改造成会议室的房源。当然，还有史蒂夫·乔布斯。伟大领导者的一个共同特质就是对细节的极度关注，而一旦他们放手某些事务，关注点可能就会转移。你觉得是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Yeah, that's such a great point. You mentioned the Jobs example and there's a great book that you've probably read or in your community seen, I believe it's called Creative Selection by Ken Kocienda about the early days of the iPhone, and I think it was Project Purple or something like that, and you're absolutely right. There wasn't no slides, none of this. They brought in the prototypes for each of those reviews and things like how to do typing on a tiny screen and those early keyboards and how to do auto complete, and Jobs was totally in those details from Ken's telling in this book.
turns.zh: 是的，你说得太对了。你提到了乔布斯的例子，我相信你读过或在你的圈子里听说过肯·科西恩的《创意精选》，这本书讲述了iPhone早期开发的故事，当时叫“紫色项目”。正如肯在书中所描述的，根本没有幻灯片之类的东西。他们会带来每个设计的原型，讨论如何在小屏幕上打字、早期的键盘设计、自动补全功能等等。乔布斯对每个细节都了如指掌。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, I couldn't agree with you more, and it's something that people miss because most of their exposure to leaders is on a YouTube video or at all hands, and so, they don't really get to see that side of leaders I think, and it's also not what I think from an ego perspective is kind of what people want it to be about. They want to be about making big decisions or commanding a large group of people, and I think it's hard to do that without these pieces.
turns.zh: 所以我完全赞同你的观点。人们往往忽视了这一点，因为他们对领导者的了解大多来自YouTube视频或全体会议之类的。所以他们看不到领导者的这些侧面，而从自我形象的角度来看，这也并非人们所期望的。人们总觉得领导者应该做重大决策、指挥大批员工，但我认为，如果没有这些细节，这些都很难实现。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: One other thing I just wanted to briefly touch on to your point on how they're connected, it's a really good point, and at the surface it almost seems like they could potentially be the same thing. One thing worth calling out though I think is the idea of something not being above somebody or a person not being above things. I think the biggest thing I take away from that is humility is that nothing is not my job, right? Anything, could be picking up paper off the floor and putting it in the trash, or it could be reviewing a product spec, whatever it is, and then begin the details in my opinion is about craft, right, and really understanding things at a low level such that you're able to reason about it and make good decisions, like Brian with the homepage or Bezos in some cases with customer processes that he got in the weeds on. I think the two together, humility and being excellent at craft, I think is a very potent combination, especially when you throw in the last thing of being able to adapt to any situation.
turns.zh: 关于他们如何相互关联这一点，我还想简要谈谈您的观点，您的观点非常深刻。从表面看来，他们似乎可能是一回事。但有一点值得强调，那就是某物不凌驾于某人之上，或者说某人不凌驾于事物之上。我认为从中领悟到的最重要一点是谦逊——即没有什么事情不属于我的职责范围。无论是捡起地上的纸扔进垃圾桶，还是审核产品规格，抑或处理其他细节，在我看来，这都关乎精湛技艺。只有真正深入理解事物的底层逻辑，才能进行合理分析并做出明智决策，比如布莱恩设计主页时的考量，或贝索斯在客户流程中深陷困境的经历。在我看来，谦逊与精湛技艺相结合，是一股强大的力量，尤其是当你能适应任何情境时。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's really interesting. What it also makes me think about is the reason things are less good often if there isn't a person at the top that's being very detail-oriented, and I find this with the newsletter and this podcast and other stuff is no one's going to care as much about it. No one's going to be like, "Oh my god, I really need to get this right so much because I'm just like, I'm personally feeling responsible for the quality of this stuff and it's like it's on my shoulders to make this awesome." And so, I think that's probably why a lot of the best stuff is led by a singular leader or singular opinion or singular person. A lot of the best startups are just someone's vision is like, "Here, this is what we're going to do," and then the more it becomes a community-driven thing, the less often it ends up being successful.
turns.zh: 这真的很有趣。这也让我想到，如果没有一位高层领导对细节高度关注，事情往往会做得很糟糕。我在通讯和播客等领域的经验表明，没有人会对此足够上心。没人会说：“天哪，我必须把这件事做得完美无缺。”因为我会觉得：“这件事的质量关乎我的个人责任，必须由我来把它做到极致。” 所以，我认为这或许就是为什么很多优秀成果都由一位杰出领导者、独特观点或个别人物主导的原因。许多顶尖初创公司都源于某个创始人的愿景，比如“就这样吧，我们要这样做”，然后当它演变成社区驱动的项目时，成功的可能性就大大降低了。

Maven is a cohort-based learning platform where you learn alongside peers with a direct connection to your instructor.
