turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I feel like you're totally right, especially, I mean this is the natural progression, but it doesn't have to be that way right? And I think to your point, I think a lot of leaders focus on accountability in an organization once they get large, and so, you see things like performance reviews and things like this. It's a very top-down approach to trying to drive results, but is opposed to a sense of accountability if you drove a sense of responsibility. If people felt like this is my company too, this is my product, this is my office floor. I don't want trash on the floor. I'm going to pick it up and throw it there. Even if we have somebody whose job it supposedly is to clean that up, it's like I take pride of ownership in this and I'm connected to it, and I think that makes all the difference in terms of... At Airbnb, I think people who felt that way were willing to push back on certain things, or they're willing to propose new ideas because they felt invested in the company.
turns.zh: 我觉得你说得太对了，尤其是，我是说，这是一种自然的发展过程，但不一定非得如此，对吧？我认为你提到的观点很重要——很多领导者在企业规模扩大后才开始关注组织内的问责制，所以你会看到绩效评估之类的措施。这是一种自上而下的方法，试图推动成果达成，但如果能培养出责任感，那就完全不同了。如果员工觉得“这也是我的公司”、“这是我的产品”、“这是我的办公区域”，我不想看到地板上有垃圾，我会主动捡起来扔掉。即便有专人负责清理，我也会为此感到自豪，觉得自己与公司息息相关。我认为这种归属感能极大地改变局面……在Airbnb，我发现那些有这种意识的人愿意对某些事提出质疑，或者提出新想法，因为他们对公司投入了感情。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I see it at Alchemy all the time. I see an engineer hop in and fix something at 3:00 AM because they feel committed to the code base, and it's not a thousand-person engineering organization where my only job is to make the iOS app 2% more effective at engaging users.
turns.zh: 我在Alchemy经常看到这样的例子。比如某位工程师凌晨三点主动修复漏洞，因为他对代码库有责任感。这里可不是那种千人工程团队，我唯一的职责就是让iOS应用在用户参与度上提升2%。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, you touched on the skill of pushing back on a founder or CEO, and I know that's something you're really good at. I've seen you do this. I'm curious what you've learned about how to effectively do that as a PM at a company pushing back on a CEO or founder when you disagree.
turns.zh: 你提到了向创始人或CEO提出异议的技巧，我知道你在这方面很擅长。我见证过你的做法。我很好奇，作为产品经理，当你与CEO或创始人意见不合时，如何有效地做到这一点。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I mean, I think this is one of... I actually think it's one of the most misunderstood terms in a sense because I think language like we were talking about earlier is so important, and yet what you call something ends up defining I think 90% of what people understand about a concept, right? And so, pushback is, I couldn't imagine a word more viscerally that makes you feel like you're sort physically going against what somebody else wants, and it gears people into a mindset of then, well, how should I push back. It starts from a place of I need to disagree, I need to say no. It's a very negative mindset, purely based on the word that has come to label a behavior that alternatively could be about how do I shift the direction on something, or how do I help the business actually succeed when I disagree with somebody about something, and that's a very different mindset.
turns.zh: 我认为这是一个最被误解的术语之一，因为我们之前讨论的用词非常重要。然而你对某个事物的称呼，往往决定了人们对这个概念的90%理解，对吧？所以“pushback”这个词，让人不由自主地联想到你正在反抗别人的意愿。这会让人们陷入一种思维定式，觉得“那我该如何反击呢？”。这种思维从一开始就是“我需要反对”、“我需要说不”。这是一种纯粹消极的思维模式，而这个词本应标注的是一种行为——比如，当你不同意某个决策时，如何调整方向，如何帮助企业成功。这完全是两种不同的思维模式。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: And so, the two things that I've seen be most successful would be, I think number one is actually understanding what a goal is or what somebody's kind of issue is with something, and then actually aligning those things in some way. So, in coming back to Airbnb, I remember Airbnb had bought a company, Luxury Retreats. There was a goal to integrate that business and that product into the full Airbnb suite, and there was a lot of potential with that, but I remember that there was part of the product experience that was oriented around chatting with somebody and the idea that the business had had a very large team of wonderful people who helped you as concierges basically for your trip, and so, this was a team that I was on that, to be honest, had fairly low morale. It's always difficult to integrate an acquisition with a company, especially when we were based in different places, et cetera.
turns.zh: 所以，我见过最成功的两种方法是：首先，理解目标或对方的诉求，然后以某种方式达成共识。回到Airbnb，我记得Airbnb收购了Luxury Retreats公司。目标是将该业务和产品整合到Airbnb的全套服务中，这本有巨大潜力，但当时产品体验中有一部分是围绕与客服聊天展开的，而Luxury Retreats团队原本由一群出色的人组成，他们基本充当旅行助手。但这个团队的士气低落。整合收购公司总是困难的，尤其是我们分处不同地域等原因。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I remember hearing from a leader who had been at Airbnb for a while who's very effective at persuading senior leadership, and they understood why this was a problem because this chat product was growing in complexity. You'd have to build all these features into it, and nobody could successfully shift the direction, and as a result, it was just this... It was a mess as a result, and there was very low morale because we were taking on too much scope, people weren't sure it was the right product, it was being built up as one giant launch as opposed to an iterative thing. And what was really interesting was that this leader was very effective at understanding that the goal wasn't about building a bunch of features. It was about, as often discussed at Airbnb, a magical experience.
turns.zh: 我记得曾听一位在Airbnb工作多年的高管讲过，他非常善于说服高层领导。当时他们意识到，这个聊天产品正变得越来越复杂。必须要把各种功能都整合进去，但没人能成功调整方向，最终导致项目一团乱麻。士气低落的原因在于，我们承担了过多的开发任务，人们不确定这是否是正确的产品，而且这个项目被当作一次大规模的发布，而不是一个迭代的过程。最有趣的是，这位领导者深知关键不在于堆砌功能，而是要实现Airbnb常说的"魔法般的体验"。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: And so, when we took a step back, it was reimagined as trip designers, not concierges, and their goal was to design your trip, and part of that meant a very elegant, simple chat experience so that you could have a efficient, fast, positive experience with that trip designer and move on. And it shifted the pushback of like, "We can't build this thing, it's too many features, we don't have enough time, we don't have enough resources" to, "Oh, we all want a really elegant, really smooth, slick experience for our customers. How do we do that? What's a trip design or a new concept that is actually going to elevate things? We're not telling you we want a payback scope. We're not saying we want to settle for less. We're actually just not only going to call it something different, but also envision a simpler experience which is more elegant. It's more on brand with luxury."
turns.zh: 于是，当我们退后一步重新构思时，我们将其重新定位为"旅行设计师"而非"礼宾服务"。他们的目标是为用户设计专属旅程，而这其中就包括打造简洁优雅的聊天体验，让用户能高效、快速、愉快地与旅行设计师互动，并继续推进后续流程。这种转变让人们不再抗拒"功能太多""时间不足""资源匮乏"等借口，而是达成了共识："我们都想为客户提供极致简洁、流畅的体验。如何实现？旅行设计或新概念能否提升用户体验？我们不是要求缩减功能范围，也不是降低标准。我们要重新定义产品，构想更简洁、更优雅的体验，这才符合奢侈品品牌的调性。"

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Boom, all of a sudden, everybody gets what they want. It's a better customer experience, less scope, and it wasn't about saying no. It was about understanding what we're all actually sharing as a goal which was a great simple customer experience and then actually building that. So, I saw that to be really effective and I think that that's something I try to bring into my career. I have a couple other examples if it's useful, but that was a big one that I learned from Airbnb.
turns.zh: 结果立竿见影，人人皆得所愿。用户体验提升了，功能范围缩减了，而这并非靠拒绝，而是通过重新定义共同目标——打造卓越的客户体验，并切实落地。这些经验让我深受启发，我也努力将其融入自己的职业生涯中。若有需要，我还能举更多例子，但Airbnb的这个案例最具启发性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, another example would be great. One thought there though is do you think it was mostly the name and the concept or was it that it was a bigger idea? What do you think it was about reframing it that way that got people, "Oh wow, okay, now I'm really excited about it again"?
turns.zh: 没错，再举个例子也很好。但我有个疑问：你觉得这主要是因为名称和概念的创新，还是更深层的理念？如何通过重新构思让人们重新燃起热情？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: That's a great point. I think it was a big idea, right, with a good reframing, and I think it's like many things where there's the substance of something and then there's the communication of it. And so, this is true often, for example, if a company is changing strategy. Oftentimes people might walk away feeling like, "Yeah, I guess I kind of agree with the strategy, but the way was communicated was really poor," or vice versa, like, "Yeah, they told us in advance and they sat us down all hands, but I really disagree with this strategy and I'm going to be dug into my heels and not disagree and commit now."
turns.zh: 这个问题很深刻。我认为这是一个宏大的理念，加上巧妙的重新构思。很多事情都是如此，比如公司战略调整。人们常会离开时感叹"战略理念不错，但沟通不到位"，或者反之"提前沟通，召开全员会议，但我就是不同意这个战略，宁愿固守己见也不愿妥协"。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, in this case, I think you're totally right. If it was just window dressing of... Founders are too smart, especially at all these companies we've talked about, to be fooled with a simple renaming of something. But I think the combination of a bigger idea, more exciting idea that was at the heart of what we were all going after together, combined with a simple way of communicating it because I've also seen big ideas that are poorly communicated fall flat on their face and not achieve the intended outcome. Those two together, I think were a really potent combination.
turns.zh: So, in this case, I think you're totally right. If it was just window dressing of... Founders are too smart, especially at all these companies we've talked about, to be fooled with a simple renaming of something. But I think the combination of a bigger idea, more exciting idea that was at the heart of what we were all going after together, combined with a simple way of communicating it because I've also seen big ideas that are poorly communicated fall flat on their face and not achieve the intended outcome. Those two together, I think were a really potent combination.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I'd love to hear another example.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我很想再听一个例子。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Yeah, for sure. So, a recent example at Alchemy actually, right? We're growing, we're hiring, but there are a lot of roles, especially being in Web3 that are not yet created. For example, there's traditionally growth, product growth marketing, we've created new area around growth operations which I'd be happy to talk about if we want to get into it. But it's a really interest interesting area, and we were going back and forth on should we hire for this role, it's not even a real thing. We've looked at some candidates, we're not so sure about them. And when I realize with our founders who are incredibly smart, very talented, have built the company over so many years now, they want to win. That's what they care about at the end of the day. They are so driven to win at the end of the day.
turns.zh: 是的，当然了。举个最近在Alchemy的例子吧，对吧？我们正在发展壮大，招聘员工，但有很多职位，比如Web3领域的职位，至今仍未被正式设立。比如传统的增长团队、产品增长团队、营销团队，我们还新设了增长运营部门，如果大家感兴趣的话，我很乐意详细介绍。但这确实是个很有意思的领域。我们曾反复纠结是否要招聘这个岗位，毕竟它甚至还不是一个成熟的职位。我们面试了一些候选人，但都不是很理想。后来我意识到，我们的创始团队非常聪明、才华横溢，历经多年打造了这家公司，他们一心想赢。归根结底，这才是他们最关心的——他们对胜利充满渴望。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: And so, ultimately, it wasn't like, "Let me make some rational argument about the role of growth operations or let me defend some issues with this person's resume that maybe you're spotting when we make this hiring decision," but, "Oh, you want to win? Oh, we want to grow faster? Awesome. This is the way to do it, and that's how we're going to actually become the generational company we want to be." Again, a reframing in this case around, yeah, we might disagree or squabble about certain things at a detail level, but I understand what we all came here to do and let's focus on that and how this is a part of that versus just focusing on maybe the means to an end versus the end itself, and the end always brings a lot of clarity in my experience.
turns.zh: 所以，最终的决定不是基于“让我用理性论证增长运营的角色”或者“让我反驳候选人简历中的某些问题”之类的，而是“哦，你想赢？哦，我们想更快发展？太棒了。这就是方法，这就是我们要成为一代伟大公司的秘诀。” 再说一次，在这种情况下要重新定义问题：没错，我们可能在细节上会有分歧或争执，但我理解我们来这儿的初衷，让我们聚焦于此，关注这如何成为目标的一部分，而不是执着于达成目标的手段本身。以我的经验来看，最终的目标总是能带来清晰的思路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's cool about both these examples, and another guest touched on this, when you're trying to influence the CEO or the founder, coming back to your working backwards concept, you almost want to work backwards from what are they excited about, how do they see the world, what's important to them, and then pitch it that way. So, in the first example, I imagine they were pitching to Brian and he's like, "Yeah, drip design, that sounds like something Brian would love." Then in the second example, "Yeah, we're going to win. Here's how we win." So, that's a really interesting takeaway there.
turns.zh: 这两个例子都很棒，另一位嘉宾也提到了这一点。当你试图影响CEO或创始人时，回归到你的逆向思维模式，你几乎要从他们的热情所在、他们的世界观、对他们重要的事物入手，然后以此为切入点进行说服。比如第一个例子，我想他们是向Brian推销的，Brian会说：“是啊，滴灌设计，这听起来正是Brian会喜欢的项目。” 第二个例子则是：“是啊，我们要赢。以下是我们的策略。” 这确实是很有启发的经验。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I mean, I think we all forget that we're all just humans, and at the end of the day, we all are busy, et cetera. It reminds me of a lot of sales, right? I was very unsuccessful when I was trying to do outbound sales in the early days of my last startup do.com because I didn't understand this. I'm a product person. I'm not a sales person. I didn't listen to what people cared about. I didn't kind of work backwards from what a CRO or head of people that we might have been selling to cared about. I was just about features and here's what we can do for you and this and that. But all they cared about were one or two things, right? Maybe the CRO's growing revenue. Maybe the head of peoples worried about culture or scaling their talent organization, and we were nowhere near that list.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我觉得我们都忘了，我们不过是普通人，说到底，大家都很忙，诸如此类的事情。这让我想起很多销售场景，对吧？在我的上一家创业公司do.com早期阶段，我做外呼销售时非常不成功，因为我没理解这个道理。我是产品人，不是销售型人才。我没有倾听客户的真正需求，也没有从客户的需求倒推，比如首席营收官（CRO）或人力资源主管的关注点究竟何在。我只是一味地强调产品功能，强调我们能为你做什么之类的。但客户真正关心的只有一两个点，比如CRO如何提升营收，人力资源主管又如何关注企业文化或人才规模扩张，而我们却完全偏离了这些核心诉求。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: And so, I think it's similar for CEOs, and there's a huge disconnect when say a PM walks into a meeting with the CEO and they're talking about something that CEO is 10 miles away from thinking about, and certainly even the mindset that they're bringing to the conversation is totally different. I think Casey made a lot of great points about this in the recent podcast as well.
turns.zh: 说到CEO们，情况也类似。当产品经理去和CEO开会时，若谈论的内容与CEO的关注点相差十万八千里，甚至带来的思维模式截然不同，那就注定会产生巨大的沟通隔阂。凯西（Casey）在最近的播客中对此也提出了很多深刻见解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. Casey Winters, podcast plug. Okay, so something else that you're really good at is you don't kind of focus career-wise on working your way up the ladder and being like the top PM, and you seem to be really good at kind of following with what's interesting to you and your interest and your curiosity. Is there something that you've learned there, something you could share for folks that are just like, "Oh my gosh, should I just keep in with this job and work my way up? Should I try something new?" What have you learned about that sort of thinking?
turns.zh: 太棒了。接下来聊聊你特别擅长的一点——你不执着于在职业生涯中步步高升，成为顶级产品经理，而是顺着自己感兴趣的方向前行。这方面你有什么心得吗？对于那些纠结于“要不要继续现在的工作、努力晋升，还是尝试新挑战”的人，你能分享些建议吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: There's the framework I like is ladder versus map, and I think that you can be either person that any point in your life. Sometimes there's a bit of a set mindset that somebody might have one way or another, but I like ladder versus map. Ladder is about moving up. It's more influence, more power, a higher title, things like this, whereas map is I just want to go wherever's interesting, right? I literally think of it, I think of my career very similar to travel. I want to go to Greece. I want to be hungry, walking around in India, sweating in a hundred degree weather. I want to go to Australia and kind of get locked out of my hotel and see what that's like.
turns.zh: 我喜欢用“阶梯式思维”和“地图式思维”来区分两种职业路径。在人生的不同阶段，每个人可能倾向于其中一种，但我更推崇“地图式思维”。阶梯式思维意味着不断攀升，追求更大的影响力、权力和头衔等外在因素；而地图式思维则强调追随兴趣，探索未知。比如我把职业生涯比作旅行——我想去希腊，想在印度汗流浃背地探索，想在澳大利亚被锁在酒店门外体验各种趣事。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I'm okay with discomfort because it's interesting. Sometimes, for better or worse, maybe this is a privilege, it's certainly a privileged thing to say, but I care more about living a really interesting life than let's say a good or comfortable life. I think that's where the growth comes from. That's where the stories come from. That's to me the things that I'll remember the most.
turns.zh: 我能接受不适感，因为那意味着有趣的体验。无论好坏（说实话，这可能是一种特权），我更在意过上充实有趣的生活，而非安稳舒适的生活。我认为这才是成长的源泉，也是人生故事的素材，这些经历将永远刻在我的记忆里。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: And so, when I think about product and I'm on my deathbed, I'm going to care about the products I built and how they affected people. Nobody's really going to be looking at my LinkedIn, hopefully for their sake and mine, at my funeral. Sorry, it's a very morbid analogy, but I think thinking of the future provides a lot of clarity about what am I going to care about a long time from now, and I think that applies to all facets of life. That's how I thought about my life partner. That's how I think about my career. That's how I think about where I want to live, San Francisco. San Francisco, a lot of people like to talk negatively about it, but I believe in the community. I believe in the place I'm interested in the long term, even if you know the short term it has some challenges to it.
turns.zh: 因此，当我躺在临终病床上回顾产品事业时，我会关注自己打造的产品及其对人们的影响。希望为了自己和他人，人们在我的葬礼上不会翻看我的领英主页。抱歉，这听起来有些冷酷，但我认为思考未来能让人清晰地认识到，未来很久以后我会真正在意什么——这一点适用于生活的方方面面。这也是我选择人生伴侣的考量标准，也是我规划职业生涯的思路，也是我决定定居旧金山的初衷。尽管许多人对旧金山诸多非议，但我相信这座城市的社区精神，相信它作为我长期关注的焦点，即便短期内它面临诸多挑战。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, I personally believe really strongly in this kind of ladder versus map distinction, and I think a lot of people are very intentional in the micro. They think about their next job, their next title, how much salary and equity there is. In good ways too, they think about the team that they're going to work on next with, but they're very unintentional about the macro. What's the big picture? What do I care about as an individual? There's not a lot of classes for that. There's not a lot of blog posts in the product management field about the touchy-feely side of this, and who are you as a person, where do you get energy from. So, for me, I found that really clarifying and it makes career decisions that have seemed risky to other people seem inevitable to me.
turns.zh: 所以，我个人非常认同“阶梯式思维”与“地图式思维”的区分。我注意到许多人在微观层面深思熟虑——他们关注下一份工作、下一个头衔、薪资与股权分配。这种关注本无可厚非，他们也会精心挑选下一个合作团队，但在宏观层面却疏于思考：大局如何？我作为个体真正在意什么？这方面的课程寥寥无几，产品管理领域也很少有博文探讨这些情感层面的议题，比如个人的价值观、能量来源等。对我而言，这种思维方式极具启发性，让那些在他人眼中看似冒险的职业决策在自己看来变得顺理成章。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a story of or example of how you use this approach to make a decision at where you end up going, and/or or is there something that you maybe regret or are really happy with in terms of the kind of the fork in the road, looking back, using this way of thinking?
turns.zh: 你能否举例说明如何运用这种方法做出人生决策？或者在人生分岔路口回首往事时，哪些选择让你后悔或倍感欣慰？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: A few concrete examples, actually. I'll keep them brief though. One is when I first moved to San Francisco, and I had mentioned I did a small sale of that education company, and I could have done a lot of more productive things with my career in the short term. I had all my peers from college who had gone off to their great jobs at Google or whatever. I said, "I'm looking to move to San Francisco and work at my dining table, and I have a little bit of savings from this, so why not? Let's see. It's going to be super interesting." I mean, it was also very boring at times, and so, I didn't want a lot on the sort of micro level, but I built five or six products. I became much better at programming as a result.
turns.zh: 事实上，我有几个具体例子。不过我会长话短说之一。刚搬到旧金山时，我提到曾出售过一家教育公司，本可以利用那段宝贵时间提升职业发展。但身边的大学好友纷纷在谷歌等大厂大展宏图，而我却选择留在旧金山，在餐桌旁工作，靠着那笔交易的微薄积蓄试水未知。当时确实有些无聊，但在微观层面我收获颇丰——开发了五六款产品，编程能力也突飞猛进。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I remember one time, it's kind of a goofy story, but I was working at my dining table, and I saw Ron Conway on the street. I was disheveled because I was just working from my apartment and I wanted to go pitch Ron Conway on this terrible idea for a startup, and so went out there, and maybe it was fortunate to not shove me to the side, and he listened to me for a minute and then I emailed him after. These are random things that happen that over time I think make us who we are. Are you the sort of person who's going to hustle and do that? When I was building that education company, I went and put flyers in people's cars in various high schools, and I was trying to get things started, and coming back to leadership, that would be below most people. It's like, "Wait, you own a company and you're sticking flyers in people's windshields?" It was like, "What's wrong with you?"
turns.zh: 我记得有一次，这算是个挺趣的事儿。我当时正在餐桌前工作，突然看到罗恩·康威在街上。我当时头发乱糟糟的，因为刚从公寓里出来工作，想去向罗恩推销一个糟糕的创业点子。我走到街上，也许幸运的是对方没把我推开。他听我讲了一分钟，之后我给他发了邮件。这些随机发生的小事儿，久而久之塑造了我们如今的模样。你会是那种愿意拼命去争取机会的人吗？我在创办教育公司时，曾去各个高中把传单塞进人们的车里，我试图把事情启动起来。而说到领导力，这对大多数人来说可能太低级了。人们会问：“等等，你拥有一家公司，却还在往人们的挡风玻璃上塞传单？”他们会说：“你到底怎么回事？”

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, anyway, I think that was an example of time where it was like, "Okay, if I'm on the ladder," I'm like, "I got to get the best entry-level job or whatever." Even if I had been an entrepreneur before that, I would've thought about my structure in my career, and I was more like, "This is going to be interesting. I'll figure it out. I believe in myself enough that I'll figure it out." So, I did that. Yammer and leaving Yammer was similar where I could have stayed. My equity was finally worth something. I could have learned a lot even I'm sure from the Microsoft structure, but I was bored and I had been talking to a couple angel investors who were willing to put money into whatever the thing was going to be, and I felt like raising money's actually going to be really hard for me. This is going to make my life a lot easier and I can focus on product and so on and so forth.
turns.zh: 总之，我觉得这就是个例子，说明当你身处某个位置时，就得说：“好吧，如果我要往上爬，”我就会想：“我得找份最棒的入门级工作，或者别的什么。”即使我之前就创业过，也会考虑职业规划。但我当时更倾向于说：“这会很有趣。我能应付得来。我足够相信自己能解决问题。”所以我这么做了。离开Yammer的经历也类似，我本可以留下来。但我的股权终于有了价值。即便我确信能从微软的架构中学到很多东西，我还是觉得无聊，而且我一直在和几位天使投资人交流，他们愿意为我的项目注资。但我觉得筹钱对我来说实在太难了。这样反倒让我生活轻松许多，可以专注于产品开发等等。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: That was a really hard four years. Things like an M&A offer falling through the day before your wedding, or chewing glass and submitting to the Apple iStore and being a featured app and then resubmitting because we wanted to fix a bug, and then actually now it crashes 90% of the time. It's Memorial Day weekend and you can't get in touch with the Apple business development manager who can help you out to reapprove something. It was a really stressful four years, but using the map analogy, that's like getting lost in Croatia and having to find your way out or getting lost to to your hotel in Australia or getting bitten by a dog in Thailand, which actually did happen to me. But these are interesting experiences that I think build characters.
turns.zh: 那真是艰难的四年。像婚礼前一天M&A交易泡汤，或者在苹果应用商店提交应用被推荐，又因为要修复漏洞重新提交，结果现在90%的时候都会崩溃。阵亡将士纪念日周末联系不上能帮忙重新审批的苹果业务开发经理。真是压力山大的四年，但用地图作比喻，就像在克罗地亚迷路不得不找路出来，或者在澳大利亚找不到酒店，又或者在泰国被狗咬了（这事儿真发生在我身上）。但这些都是有趣的经历，我觉得它们塑造了性格。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, I'll pause there, but I think there are a lot of career decisions I've made. Do I have regrets? At times, for sure because you see what would've happened if you had joined a different company at that time and it would've been like, "Oh, I would've met so many great people. I would've worked on these products. I mean, my equity would've been worth more," whatever. But I think you only lived once, and I think that these rare experiences have been very true to me and taught me things that I wouldn't learn otherwise.
turns.zh: 所以我先说到这儿，但我觉得自己做过很多职业决策。有遗憾吗？当然有时候会有，因为你会想，如果当时加入了另一家公司，可能会遇到很棒的人，参与那些产品项目，我的股权价值也会更高之类的。但我觉得人生只有一次，这些难得的经历对我来说意义非凡，让我学到了其他地方学不到的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's really cool about that analogy, ladder versus map, is a lot of times you think you're climbing a ladder and you think it's innately going to be great, and sometimes that ladder falls over and the company doesn't go anywhere and/or the job sucks, your ladder's heading to some terrible place. And what I find in my experience is anytime I try something totally new and take a risk, especially following things that give me energy, and I'm just like, "Let's just take a leap on this thing," in my experience at least, it's always led to better opportunities and much more interesting work. And so, it's kind of this get off the ladder to get on a different ladder, and sometimes you think you're on a nice ladder and it's not going to get you anywhere anyway. So, explore other ladders. So, I'm kind of picturing a Chutes and Ladders.
turns.zh: 这种类比——把职业生涯比作攀登阶梯和探索地图——真的很妙。很多时候，你以为自己正在攀登阶梯，认为这条路注定会通向成功，但有时阶梯会突然倒塌，公司停滞不前，工作又令人不满。以我的经验来看，每当我尝试全新的事物、勇于冒险，尤其是追随那些能激发我热情的方向时，总能收获更好的机遇和更有趣的工作。所以，关键在于跳下原来的阶梯，转向新的机遇。有时你以为自己走在不错的阶梯上，但它终究无法带你去往理想之地。所以，要去探索其他阶梯。这让我联想到《跳棋与阶梯》（Chutes and Ladders）这个游戏。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's many ladders and you want to explore the different ladders across the map. How about that?
turns.zh: 地图上有很多阶梯，你需要探索不同的阶梯。怎么样？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I mean, I think you're totally right, and the only brief thing I would add to the way that you put it which I think captures the essence here is I think we all have a lot of false precision about what we think a given career move is going to lead to or what it's going to be like, and we forget that a lot of career decisions are made out of maybe 10 hours cumulatively talking to a team and getting signals.
turns.zh: 我觉得你说得太对了。唯一想补充的一点是，我们对职业变动的预期往往过于确定，忘记了许多职业决策实际上是基于与团队沟通10个小时后得到的信号而做出的。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, I think that that false precision sometimes gives us comfort in making certain decisions and folds us back from a bolder decision that might be better, but maybe the ladder is just hidden behind some fog if you really want that, and you can get both. Maybe you can go to the most interesting place in the world, and have the success in life and progress and so on and so forth. It's just that I think a lot of people think it's totally either/or. They think that they've already figured out the precise outcome that's going to happen, and to your point, the ladder often does fall over. If that's what all your hopes are pinned on, it's a very fragile career decision I think is really difficult to navigate.
turns.zh: 所以，我认为这种虚假的确定性有时会让我们安于现状，错失更大胆的选择。也许阶梯隐藏在迷雾之后，只要你真心渴望，就能两者兼得。或许你能登上世界最有趣的舞台，收获人生成功与进步。关键是，很多人认为二者非此即彼。他们以为早已预知了未来的结果，但正如你所说，阶梯往往会倒塌。如果这就是你全部的希望寄托，那这就是个脆弱的职业决策，确实难以把握。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The flip side, you also don't want to be bouncing around over and over and over. As much as I talked about how I shifted and tried new things, I'm a very serial monogamous in terms of work. My first job, I was there nine years, then a startup for a year and a half, and then Airbnb for seven years, and then what I'm doing now may be forever. And so, there's a lot of value to sticking around and kind of seeing things through. And so, I guess, I don't know if you'll have an answer to this, but do you have any wisdom on when to stick with it and keep exploring opportunities at a place you're at versus trying something new?
turns.zh: 另一方面，你也不想频繁跳槽。虽然我谈到自己多次转换和尝试新事物，但在工作方面我是个高度专注的人。我第一份工作做了九年，然后在一家初创公司待了一年半，接着在Airbnb待了七年，而现在的工作可能也会一直做下去。所以，坚持下去、把事情做完也有很大价值。所以，我不知道你是否能回答这个问题，但对于在现有岗位上继续探索机会还是尝试新事物，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: My hope is that there's a balance here in the sense that the map shouldn't give the impression of 180 countries, let's do 180 tech companies and shorten the tenure from two years down to a month, and we've just created a generation of job hoppers which is even easier because we're all on Zoom. It's a good point and I really respect people like you who have stuck it out through the ups and the downs and somebody sees seven years on paper, but I mean, seven years, I don't know. How many chapters of Airbnb, how many crises moments?
turns.zh: 我希望能找到平衡点。地图不应给人留下180个国家、180家科技公司、将任期从两年缩短至一个月的印象。我们正在培养一代跳槽族，而Zoom会议让这一切变得更容易。这是个好观点，我非常尊重像你这样在风雨中坚守的人——七年的工作经历固然值得尊敬，但七年呢？Airbnb经历了多少个篇章，又经受过多少次危机考验？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Felt like 300.
turns.zh: 感觉像300次。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: There you go. So, I think there's a balance, right? For example, I want to be in Web3 for more than a decade. I want to stay at Alchemy for a very long time and help build the company. So, I guess when I think of map, maybe an important way to think about it is maybe when somebody is 50 or 60 or 70 and they might choose to stop working, a lot of people when they start their career actually have 30 years to play with or 40 years or 50 if they're lucky. That's a lot of chips you can play. You could do five, 10 year rounds, right? And so, I think that in terms of sticking it out, maybe I'm biased, I think that some of the absolute sort gems, if you will, in Silicon Valley and tech are the teammates that are willing to stay around for 4, 5, 6, 7 years, and they have institutional knowledge that nobody has. They have a positive impact on the culture that is impossible if there's constant employee turnover.
turns.zh: 就是这样。所以，我觉得这里面有一种平衡，对吧？比如说，我想在Web3领域深耕十多年。我希望能在Alchemy待很久，帮助公司发展。所以，我觉得当我想到职业发展路径时，或许一个重要思考方向是，当一个人50岁、60岁、70岁时，可能会选择停止工作。但很多人刚开始职业生涯时，实际上有30年、40年甚至50年的时间可以挥霍。这是大量可以利用的筹码。你可以进行5年的、10年的轮次，对吧？所以，我认为在坚持下去方面，也许我有些偏见，但硅谷和科技领域的一些绝对的精英，是那些愿意留下来4、5、6、7年的队友。他们拥有无人能及的机构知识。如果员工流动频繁，他们对公司文化的积极影响就无从谈起。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, to me, I think that you could simultaneously be somebody who's committed to companies, stays for a very meaningful amount of time, but zooms out and looks at their career. Actually, I think maybe this was even more, right? You're now a famous podcaster. You were a successful startup founder. You were a product leader. All these things form a map and I think a really interesting career and life, frankly, that's pretty full with a lot of really interesting milestones and learnings and networks and people that you get to interact with.
turns.zh: 所以，对我来说，我认为你可以同时既忠于公司，待很久，同时又能放眼全局审视自己的职业生涯。实际上，我觉得这甚至更重要，对吧？你现在是知名播客主，曾是成功的创业者，做过产品负责人。所有这些经历构成了你的职业与人生路径，坦白说，这条路径相当丰富，充满了有趣的里程碑、经验教训、人脉与交流机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. To your point about how long a career is, when I thought about it recently, this is my fourth career. First it was an engineer, then it was a founder, then a product manager when I got to Airbnb, and now this weird thing that I do, and there's so much time to explore and try new things. I will say though, I feel like the early things you do seem really important. Airbnb for me was not early, so maybe I'm wrong, but it feels like you want to work at a company where people look at that on your resume and are like, "Oh, okay, this person's probably good." So, I feel like there's that piece you got to get right at some point.
turns.zh: 是的。关于职业生涯的时长，你最近怎么看？对我来说，这是我的第四次职业转型。最初是工程师，后来成为创业者，到了Airbnb后转产品经理，现在做现在这份奇怪的工作。但还有大量时间去探索和尝试新事物。不过我得说，我觉得早期阶段的工作似乎很重要。Airbnb对我来说不算早期阶段，所以也许我错了，但感觉人们看到你简历上的这段经历时，会觉得“哦，原来这个人不错。”所以，我觉得在某个阶段，你必须把这部分做好。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Yeah, I totally agree with that. For example, I think for let's say a new grad who's thinking about a product career, and let's say on the spectrum there is maybe Goldman Sachs because that's what a lot of people are doing. They're like, "Yeah, I want to do product, but I also feel like I need this gold star or whatever." And then in between is you could join a hypergrowth company of some sort where they definitely have good product people you can learn from, but definitely still room for you to do more than what a very junior person would be assigned to be doing. And then on the other end of the spectrum is I'm going to have no job, I'm just going to completely bounce around from my own projects or just work with a new startup every two months.
turns.zh: 是的，我完全同意。比如说，对于刚毕业、想从事产品工作的学生来说，可能选择高盛之类的公司，因为很多人都这么做。他们会想：“是的，我也想做产品，但我觉得自己需要个‘金字招牌’之类的。”而中间的路径是加入某个高速发展的公司，那里肯定有优秀的产品团队可以学习，但肯定还有提升空间，不只是初级人员能做的事。而另一端则是完全没有工作，自己做项目，或者每两个月就换一家新创业公司。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Personally in that spectrum, I tend to be more towards the middle of that where build a track record, build a network. I mean, it's crazy. Even just this week, next week I'm seeing maybe five people that I know from my Yammer days, and to your point on formative nature, some of those people, that's how I learned how to do product. That's how I learned things like AB testing. It's how I had the first angel investors in my next company. That's how I hire. I still hire people, maybe much to their chagrin, they still get LinkedIn messages for me trying to push them for the next thing.
turns.zh: 就我个人而言，在这个职业生涯发展谱上，我更倾向于处于中间阶段——积累业绩、构建人脉网络。这简直太疯狂了。就拿这周来说，我见了大概五个在Yammer时代就认识的人。你提到的成长性影响很深，其中有些人让我学会了如何做产品，比如AB测试。也是他们帮我找到了下一家公司的首批天使投资人。现在我招聘员工时，他们可能还很不爽，因为我仍会通过领英消息推销我的项目，试图说服他们加入。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, I totally agree that those early days are really formative, and there's maybe a balance between nobody wants to be a job hopper, but at the same time maybe there's ways to also not just be a career person who spends kind of 30 years working up the ladder or is fixated on I need to be CPO but is willing to give up a director title to go be a hustler at some startup because they really believe in it and they want to take a bet or risk in their career.
turns.zh: 所以我完全认同早期职业生涯的塑造作用，也许需要在不做跳槽狂魔和一心攀升职业阶梯之间找到平衡。比如有些人执着于成为CPO，却愿意放下总监头衔，加入初创公司去拼搏，因为他们真正相信这个事业，愿意为职业生涯冒险一试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You touched on hiring, and that's something I wanted to ask you. So, you're in my Talent Collective. You're a company that's hiring, Alchemy, and I was looking at the stats recently, and you're one of the most successful companies at getting candidates to talk to you, and generally I think you're just really good at hiring. So, I'm curious what you can share with folks about hiring.
turns.zh: 你提到了招聘，这正是我想问的。你加入了我的Talent Collective，Alchemy作为招聘公司，最近我看数据发现，你们是吸引候选人交流最成功的公司之一，总体来说你们在招聘方面做得很棒。我很好奇能否分享一些招聘心得。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I appreciate that, and I get a lot of value out of meeting some really talented people from the Collective. I think hiring, it's funny, it reminds me of sort of push back in a sense of what you call it has such an impact on how people think about it. It's hiring, recruiting, but if people reframe it as the people you are going to work with every day or the people who make the company what it is, it shifts the mindset. It's like how is that not the most important thing to be thinking about as a leader or as a founder. A lot of people have benchmarks. I think maybe on the Google podcast I talk about 30%, 40% of a founder's time maybe spent on recruiting because I think deep down everybody understands that that's incredibly valuable.
turns.zh: 很感激能结识Collective中这么多才华横溢的人。我觉得招聘这事很有意思，人们对它的看法其实受很多偏见影响。比如把招聘视为必要之恶，但如果把它重新定义为未来共事的伙伴、成就公司的核心力量，思维方式就会完全不同。作为领导者或创始人，招聘难道不是最重要的优先级吗？很多人有招聘比例指标，比如我在Google播客中提到，创始人可能需要30%到40%的时间用于招聘，因为大家都深知这份投入的巨大价值。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I think that for me personally, I was reflecting ahead of the podcast on how I approach things now after different stages of hiring, and for context, for what it's worth, I've been at the zero person startup. It's just me and I'm trying to convince some Google engineer to come join us which is incredibly hard and has a low hit rate, to a place like Amazon or Airbnb where you have a large world-class recruiting organization that is effectively doing sourcing for you and setting up interviews and such things like this, and there's formal calibrations and interview panels, to a place like Alchemy where it's very sort of scrappy. We need to figure out who we even want to hire. The founders still meet with every candidate. It's a really different environment.
turns.zh: 就我个人而言，回顾播客前我反思了不同招聘阶段的经验。举例来说，我从零人创业公司起步时，只能孤身说服谷歌工程师加入，成功率极低；到亚马逊或爱彼迎这样拥有专业招聘团队的公司，招聘流程规范；再到Alchemy这样资源有限的初创公司，我们需要亲自面试候选人。每个阶段都带来不同挑战。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, this is kind of the spectrum that I've seen, and I was reflecting what do I think works the best, and I like to think of it in very similar motions to a business where I think there is a marketing aspect to it, there was a sales aspect, and there is a product aspect to it. What I mean by that is that on a marketing level, I think what has a person heard about your company. Do they know anybody who works there? Do they read your LinkedIn post about things and already know that you're a known quantity before they even step in the door to interview? Are they even willing to interview based on what they know about the company? And so, I think that the marketing aspect in it, and I mean it's sort of lower case marketing in this sense of course because I think a hard sell of any sort or anything that's not authentic is probably going to fail ultimately, but it's about developing a really positive kind of brand and reputation for a company but also as an individual.
turns.zh: 嗯，这就是我所观察到的招聘流程的全貌。我一直在思考，怎样才能做得最好？我觉得这和商业中的营销、销售、产品三要素有着相似的逻辑。就营销层面而言，关键在于人们对你的公司的了解程度。他们是否认识在那里工作的员工？他们是否通过领英动态已经对你有所了解，甚至在进入面试环节前就对你心知肚明？他们是否会因为对公司的认知而愿意接受面试？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: And then if you pass that threshold, I feel like there's a sort of a sales process, and we were talking about how bad of a salesperson I am, for example, because I didn't listen to people's pain points and understand the one or two things that were most important to them. I think similarly in this context, if they're an engineer, do they want to work in a world-class engineering organization? If they're a product person or they're just really excited about crypto and they want to find a way in, a place like Alchemy's the best place for them to learn that is how to think about it, and it's not about misdirecting on or matching whatever they say, but it's about really understanding who they are and what motivates them and what they're excited about because I'm as concerned about the kind of post-hiring step as I am the pre-hiring and want them to work out and be happy and be effective.
turns.zh: 接下来是销售环节。说到这里，我得承认自己是个不怎么样的销售，因为我总是不去倾听求职者的痛点，没能抓住对他们最重要的两三点。同理，针对工程师候选人，他们是否渴望加入世界一流的工程团队？对于产品经理或对加密领域充满热情的求职者来说，Alchemy这样的公司是他们学习思维模式的最佳平台。这里关键不在于迎合他们的表述，而是要深入理解他们的个性、驱动力和热情所在。因为我不仅关注招聘前的筛选，更关注入职后的成长——我希望新员工能适应工作环境、快乐高效地工作。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: And then lastly, I think there's a product angle to it that not a lot of people think about or talk about a lot because I think the product, it's one of those rare cases where job descriptions are almost like product specs, right? They're here's what the responsibilities are, here's what we need you to do, here's the qualifications we're looking for. And what's really funny about that is that product is very iterative, but somehow we just write a job description, and then it's bait, it's done, it's posted, and nobody thinks about it again until the person's hired and then they take it down.
turns.zh: 最后，我认为这其中还涉及一个产品视角，很多人并未深思或多谈此事，因为我觉得产品经理的职位描述，几乎是产品规格书的翻版，对吧？里面写着职责清单、要求条件等等。而最有趣的是，虽然产品开发是个不断迭代的过程，但我们却往往只是草拟一份职位描述，然后把它当作招聘广告，发布出去，之后就再也不管了，直到候选人入职后才撤下招聘信息。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I think taking a product mindset where I meet people all the time now where I don't really know exactly what role they're necessarily going to fill, I'm not really sure about exactly their seniority, maybe they don't have a lot of experience, but maybe they would just totally be a rockstar on our product team. And looking at a product that we can mold flexibly and think of the same way if at Airbnb, if we were going to build Airbnb Plus, if we just kind of came back to the Amazon working backwards and just wrote a document and it was over, that's one thing, but we didn't do that, right? We went and actually built rooms and homes that were supposed to be Airbnb Plus, and then we iterate on it and we changed the pillows and we changed the entrance and we changed the scent that you feel when you walk in. We coach host and learned about that.
turns.zh: 我现在经常接触这样的人：他们并不确定自己将承担何种角色，也不清楚自己的职级高低，可能经验不足，但或许能成为我们产品团队的核心成员。以Airbnb为例，我们曾尝试打造Airbnb Plus产品，当时若是参照亚马逊的模式，先写份文档然后直接上线，那倒是简单，但我们并没有这么做。我们实际搭建了符合Airbnb Plus标准的客房和民宿，不断优化设计——更换枕头、调整入口通道、调整入住时的香氛体验。我们还指导房东提升服务水平，并从中积累经验。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, I think a product mindset on hiring and iterating on it based on the candidates you're meeting, the needs of the business. So this kind of marketing, sales, product combination has been what I've found to be really effective at getting people excited, understanding who they are and what they need, and then crafting a role that actually makes the person successful, rather than just checks a box in your recruiting software as some new headcount that was hired.
turns.zh: 因此，我认为在招聘和迭代过程中，应秉持产品思维，基于你接触的候选人以及业务需求来进行调整。这种将市场、销售和产品三者相结合的方法，确实能有效激发人们的热情，让他们了解自身定位与需求所在，并为其量身打造一份真正助其成功的职位，而非只是在招聘系统中填写一个新员工的信息框。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One last question before we get to our lightning round. For PMs that are listening to this maybe early in their career, what skill have you found to be most important in helping you and helping PMs in general advance in their career?
turns.zh: 在进入闪电问环节之前，我还有最后一个问题。对于那些正处于职业生涯早期的产品经理们，你们认为哪项技能对个人成长和职业发展最为重要？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Yeah, this is a really important question, like the others, but I think that understanding and defining what problem matters is the most important skill that I think I've taken away, and it applies to so many things. It can apply to a specific product we're building. It can apply to what a company's mission is. I think I've found it really effective because it affects pretty much everything. It affects what we're going to build. It affects is the team motivated by what we're doing. So, specifically for example, at a place like Alchemy where, yeah, we're a developer platform, but should we build an SDK so there's abstraction that is easier for developers to use? Should we build an NFT API because we think that's a really important stack to move into and an important use case to support?
turns.zh: 嗯，这个问题和其他问题一样重要，但我认为理解并定义问题的本质是最重要的技能。这项技能适用于多个领域——无论是我们正在开发的产品，还是公司的使命宣言。我发现它对几乎所有事情都产生深远影响。它决定了我们要构建什么样的产品，决定了团队是否会被我们的目标所激励。以Alchemy为例，我们的平台面向开发者，但我们是否应该开发一个SDK来简化开发流程？是否应该开发NFT API，因为我们认为这是至关重要的技术栈和应用场景？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Well, the question is what problem are we solving? It's not this versus that just in a vacuum. It's is the problem developer experienced and we want to make things easier to develop. Is the problem that an NFT marketplace, a whole suite of them are trying to grow and need more support from us, and not understanding these problems clearly? And it goes back to my first company. It was an education company, and the problem was that low-income students didn't have access to the same resources to get into college as other students, and that guided everything. That guided the pricing model which was basically free for a long time, and then we monetize on sponsorships from colleges, right? The problem matter, whereas the problem solve was there's not a... A different problem was there's just no good college readiness program. Fine, then you focus manically on the pedagogy and the curriculum and so on and so forth, rather than say the business model and an initial product that you think can work.
turns.zh: 关键问题在于我们要解决什么样的问题。不能在真空中进行非此即彼的选择。关键在于开发者面临的实际问题，以及我们如何让开发更轻松。是NFT市场需要更多支持却缺乏清晰的理解？还是低收入学生无法获得与其他学生同等的升学资源？这让我回想起我的第一家公司——一家教育机构。当时的核心问题是低收入家庭的学生无法获得与其他学生同等的升学资源。这决定了我们的定价策略——长期免费，再通过大学赞助实现变现。问题定义决定了产品形态，而非简单地复制现有模式。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: So, that's what I've found to be the most useful, and I can give her other examples if it's helpful, but understanding what problem we're actually trying to solve and really getting crystal clear about it, I think has been incredibly useful to me and energizing as well.
turns.zh: 所以，这才是最有用的方法。如果有帮助的话，我可以举更多例子，但深刻理解我们要解决的问题并清晰界定它，对我来说极其有益，也能激发我的工作热情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's such a good reminder, even though it's such a cliche of product managers being, "Well, what problem are we trying to solve here?" People hate that, but Michael Paul, and I mentioned this on a different podcast too, he makes this point that when you do drugs sometimes, you have these epiphanies that you come out and you're like, "Love is all you need, man." It's like, okay, yep. But it feels so right. You really feel it. The reason that it's such a cliche is because people have found it to be so true for so long that it's annoying now, but it also tells you how true it is. And so, I think it's a really good reminder of yes, it's annoying to ask that question, and people make fun of PMs for that, but that's because it's so damn important.
turns.zh: 这真是个很好的提醒，尽管产品经理常被问到“我们到底要解决什么问题？”这种老生常谈的问题，人们都很反感。但迈克尔·保罗（Michael Paul）说过，他提到有时服用药物后会有顿悟时刻，比如你突然感悟“爱就是全部，伙计”。虽然听起来有点理想化，但那种感觉确实很棒。其他人之所以觉得这老掉牙，可能是因为这种真理被反复验证到令人厌烦的地步，但这恰恰说明它确实至理名言。所以我觉得这提醒我们，尽管被嘲笑老生常谈，但这种追问问题的思维方式确实至关重要。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Just a brief kind of additional, what you share there, I mean, I completely agree. I think it's very true in life, right? It's like, well, what matters? And it's like, well, your health, your family, your sense of purpose. It's like nobody's unfamiliar with the answer, but like most things, it's about the application of it and about the nuance of it, and I think that's what product is ultimately sort of all about too.
turns.zh: 你说得太对了。我完全赞同。我觉得这在生活中同样适用，对吧？比如，什么才是最重要的？答案显而易见——健康、家庭、人生目标。没人会对这些答案感到陌生，但关键在于如何践行这些真理，领会其微妙之处。我认为这正是产品经理工作的核心所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Are you ready for our lightning round where I'm just going to ask you five quick questions, tell me what comes to mind and we'll have some fun. Does that sound good?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你准备好迎接闪电问答环节了吗？我会快速问你五个问题，说出你的第一反应，应该会很有趣。对吧？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: That sounds great. Ready.
turns.zh: 好的，我觉得我要开始给这些视频加音乐了。我得先研究一下怎么操作。暂时先不加音乐。好的。你最推荐其他产品经理读哪本书？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. I think I'm going to start adding music to these things. I got to figure that out. For now, no music. Okay. What book do you recommend most to other PMs?
turns.zh: 《艰难之事》。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: The Hard Thing About Hard things.
turns.zh: 能讲讲原因吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you add why?
turns.zh: 我觉得它教会产品经理像CEO一样能吃苦耐劳，关注结果，这是一种非常有用的思维模式。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I think it teaches product managers to chew glass and care about outcomes the way that a CEO has to, and I think that's a really useful mindset to have.
turns.zh: 天啊，这个“吃苦耐劳”的比喻，我可不喜欢这个说法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Man, this chew glass metaphor, I don't like the sound of that.
turns.zh: 我看到你皱眉了。我有点担心你会不喜欢。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I saw you cringe. I was a little worried about that.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪。我们这份工作真是吃苦耐劳啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my god. What a great job we have here, chewing glass. Okay. Other than Alchemy, what's a company you recommend most to PMs to go look for new gigs if they're looking around?
turns.zh: 除了Alchemy，还有哪些公司你最推荐产品经理去寻找新机会？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I would suggest Polygon, Salon, or MoonPay. I know it's three, but I wanted to give some breath in the Web3 space that might be exciting to people.
turns.zh: Polygon、Salon或者MoonPay。我知道是三个，但我想在Web3领域推荐一些可能让人们兴奋的公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great, great choices. What's a favorite TV show or movie that you've recently watched?
turns.zh: 太棒了。爱看这个。好的。最喜欢的电视节目或电影是什么？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: The Ken Burns Vietnam War series. I'm really into documentaries and history, and it's a really kind of compelling version of history that I've never seen before.
turns.zh: 肯·伯恩斯的越战纪录片系列。我对纪录片和历史很感兴趣，这是我从未见过的一种引人入胜的历史叙事方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Love that. Okay. Favorite interview question that you like to ask.
turns.zh: 太棒了。爱看这个。好了。你最喜欢问的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: What is a risk you regret not taking, why, and what did you learn about yourself?
turns.zh: 你后悔没有抓住的风险是什么？为什么？从中你对自己有何认识？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you look for in an answer there?
turns.zh: 你对答案有什么要求？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I think the biggest thing I look for is a growth mindset, to be able to reflect on an experience like that and be vocally self-critical without unproductively being hard on one's self, and I think that the dimension of asking about risk gets at their psychology and how do they think about not only their career, but if they were to work with me, how would they approach problem solving and taking bets on the business.
turns.zh: 我认为最重要的是具备成长型思维，能够反思这样的经历，并坦诚地自我批评，而不是毫无益处地苛责自己。我觉得询问风险承受能力的环节，能洞察他们的心理状态——他们如何看待自己的职业生涯，以及如果他们与我共事，会如何处理解决问题和冒险尝试新机遇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, final question. What's your least favorite vegetable?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好，最后一个问题。你最不喜欢的蔬菜是什么？

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: Broccoli. I just removed some from a pizza last night that I really didn't want to eat.
turns.zh: 西兰花。昨晚我刚从披萨里摘下一些，我实在不想吃。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Oh wow, okay. Even like steamed, cook, all the things?
turns.zh: 哇。天哪，真得吃这些蔬菜啊。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: There are no circumstances under which I'm excited about broccoli.
turns.zh: 无论在什么情况下，我都对西兰花毫无兴趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man, you got to eat those veggies.
turns.zh: 天啊，你总得吃这些蔬菜啊。

turns.speaker: Jason Shah
turns.en: I know. I'm working on it.
